findings.claim: Legal leaders expect hourly-rate work to fall from 72% to 44% of external work within 2-3 years and 85% believe AI will change law firm pricing, yet 84% have not redesigned internal roles around AI.
findings.detail: Deloitte UK, 'The AI Imperative: Reshaping of the Legal Industry'; 121 senior legal leaders (GCs, heads of legal, legal ops directors) surveyed April-May 2026. 61% in AI deployment phases, 10% fully embedded, 2% no adoption (vs 76% in 2024); 61% piloting agentic AI; 79% raised AI investment, average +67%; expect 28% of legal work saved/automated in 2-3 years; 78% cite cost reduction as leading benefit expected from external providers. Tom Brunt quote extracted via summarizer; verify verbatim.
findings.source_title: AI set to reshape legal work, law firm pricing and legal careers
findings.exact_quote: AI is rapidly shifting from a productivity tool to a structural force in the legal sector.

findings.claim: In-house expectations of AI-driven savings from law firms are far ahead of realized savings: 64% expect reduced reliance on outside counsel and 61% plan to push for pricing/service changes, but 59% have seen no noticeable savings and only 24% are satisfied with firms' GenAI adoption.
findings.detail: ACC/Everlaw GenAI survey, 657 in-house professionals in 30 countries, fieldwork June 18-July 18 2025, released 2025-10-14. GenAI active use 52% vs 23% in 2024; 50% expect lower outside counsel costs; planned insourcing of drafting 78%, contract management 71%, research 62%; policy bans fell from 29% to 9%. Bloomberg Law coverage adds Gartner's Weston Wicks: 'Law firms don't know how to charge clients for using AI tools' (first clause of a longer sentence).
findings.source_title: 64% of In-House Counsel Expect GenAI to Reduce Reliance on Outside Counsel, 50% Expect Lower Outside Counsel Costs, ACC/Everlaw Survey Finds

findings.claim: Legal departments are ahead of their law firms on GenAI (legal research: 72.3% in-house vs 23.4% at firms) and 93.8% say AI will let them do more in-house, but fewer than one in five have pressed firms to demonstrate AI-driven savings and fewer than 40% of legal ops leaders control selection of AI legal assistants.
findings.detail: Blickstein Group / FTI Consulting 18th annual Law Department Operations Survey (68 mostly North American companies). SECONDARY: reported by Legal.io citing Legaltech News; the full Blickstein report was not retrievable. 87.5% expect reduced law firm spend; about two-thirds report ALSP spend declined; only about one-third can show measurable AI cost savings. Brad Blickstein's statement that departments lack a clear strategy for what they want from firms may be a paraphrase - verify before quoting.
findings.source_title: In-house Legal Teams Pull Ahead Of Law Firms On Generative AI Adoption

findings.claim: Despite a decade of talk, AFAs cover only about 20% of legal matters and formal law firm panels remain rare (16%); legal ops is broadening from cost control to systems, process and technology, but in 45% of cases the 'legal ops' lead is a GC doing it on the side.
findings.detail: Thomson Reuters Institute 2025 Legal Department Operations Index (PDF text read directly; July 2025 survey, 128 US respondents, with Buying Legal Council). 82% have at least one dedicated legal ops role; 56% under-resourced; 46% expect more work in-house; 73% plan to automate with advanced tech; 59% aim to improve legal-business collaboration; 70% expect GenAI to change interactions with internal stakeholders. Departments led by legal-ops professionals use more tech, ALSPs and AFAs than those led by GCs tasked with ops. Report says AFA expansion 'still remains largely a discussion rather than a plan of action'.
findings.source_title: 2025 Legal Department Operations Index
findings.exact_quote: AFAs are used in about 20% of legal matters consistently.

findings.claim: AI adoption is widespread but scaling is rare: only 7% of in-house teams have moved past pilots to using, optimizing and measuring AI; 83% cannot show whether last year's AI spend paid off; 92% expect or negotiate AI-related rate cuts from outside counsel; 52% prefer ALSPs over law firms (24%) for AI-enabled work.
findings.detail: Axiom 2026 Legal AI Survey, 528 in-house legal leaders (CLOs, GCs, DGCs, legal ops) in six countries, fielded by InsightDynamo; 77% from $1B+ companies. 66% run general-purpose AI in default configuration. Axiom is an ALSP and an interested party. Companion Axiom 2026 GC Survey (2026-02-10): 80% plan to move significant law firm work in-house or to ALSPs within 24 months. Note new title at Axiom: 'Chief Legal AI and Talent Officer' (Sara Morgan). Quote extracted via summarizer; verify.
findings.source_title: Legal AI is Everywhere, but Only 7% of Legal Teams Have Made It Work
findings.exact_quote: The technology is not the hard part. The layer around it is where value either shows up or it doesn't.

findings.claim: Client AI expectations have barely reached the contract layer: only 2% (20 of 1,054) of publicly findable outside counsel guidelines mention AI.
findings.detail: Fulkerson Advisors study of OCGs dated Dec 2022 or later found via search engines, company/insurer/public-body sites, procurement portals and court dockets. Of the 20: 12 require disclosure of AI use, 9 keep client data out of public tools, 8 require lawyer review, 9 change billing, 3 require prior approval, 1 bans AI. Named: Microsoft (2024), Zscaler (2025), UBS, The Hartford, FDIC (2026). Small consultancy; open-web sample skews toward public bodies - but it is the only hard count found. Contrast with KPMG 2026 GC Outlook: 82% expect firms to explain AI usage clearly.
findings.source_title: 2% of 1,054 Outside-Counsel Guidelines Mention AI

findings.claim: CLOC's 2026 Global Institute positioned legal ops as 'the strategic architecture behind the modern legal department'; the AI conversation shifted from possibility to governance, and CLOC launched the Compass maturity tool on the Core 12.
findings.detail: CLOC Global Institute, Chicago, May 11-14 2026, ~2,400 attendees from 26+ countries, 90+ sessions, theme 'Stronger by Design'. Program themes: AI training and governance, resource optimization/spend management, career pathways, skills, organizational design. CLOC Compass built with Neota Logic. Legal IT Insider's Toby Weston: vendors are racing to become the legal department 'operating system' with embedded AI; open question is organizational readiness. Snell quote matched in two sources. A second Snell quote (Lexpert + CCBJ): 'Legal operations leaders aren't waiting for permission anymore. They're building, proving, and leading.'
findings.source_title: CLOC Global Institute 2026: A Market in Transition
findings.exact_quote: The AI conversation has matured. Teams are now sharing what has worked, what broke, and how they are governing it.

findings.claim: New in-house roles such as 'legal engineer' are emerging inside legal ops teams, but titles, pay and headcount approval lag the work.
findings.detail: Law360 Pulse (Anna Scott Farrell). Examples: John Deere legal ops; an unnamed large pharma seeking a legal engineer for its legal ops team. Mary O'Carroll (LegalEng; former Google legal ops head and CLOC president): new, poorly understood roles make headcount approval harder. Practitioner corroboration: Gio DiLuca (Senior Director Legal Ops, Lowe's) in ACC Corporate Counsel Now, 2026-03-03, lists 'from innovator to AI governance steward' and 'from vendor management to ecosystem orchestration' among ten shifts. Quotes extracted via summarizer; verify.
findings.source_title: AI Boom Gives Rise To In-House Legal Engineers
findings.exact_quote: From what I see, the legal engineer is already in-house. We just haven't seen the title, salary shift yet.

findings.claim: AI-native law firms and hybrid AI/ALSP/law-firm providers are an established new delivery category: fixed fees, AI-first review, senior-only lawyers and no junior pyramid, enabled by Arizona ABS and UK SRA approvals; separately, Big Law is exploring MSO structures to take private equity.
findings.detail: IBA article (2025-12-11): Norm Law ($140M+ funding, Blackstone-backed, 35+ lawyers as 'legal engineers'), Crosby (58-minute median contract turnaround; later $60M Series B ~2026-04), Covenant ($900/document LPA review, ~90% below traditional), Garfield.Law (SRA-approved May 2025), Eudia Counsel (Arizona ABS). Artificial Lawyer 2026-03-31: General Legal charges $500 per contract review, $250 per NDA, 2.2-hour turnaround, 40-50% margins, hires only experienced lawyers. Artificial Lawyer 2026-01-14: Eudia (AI platform + ALSP + law firm; $105M Series A led by General Catalyst; >$20M ARR by Dec 2025). ABA Journal 2026-02-10: McDermott Will & Schulte in preliminary talks on an investor-owned MSO. Baseline: TR ALSP 2025 report sized ALSPs at $28.5B, law-firm captives only $1.8B (2025-01).
findings.source_title: The AI-native law firm: regulatory innovation and the fundamental restructuring of legal service delivery

viewpoints: CLOC / Harbor (Oyango Snell, Lauren Chung, Kevin Clem): a structural productivity gap exists; outside counsel is no longer the pressure valve; legal ops is 'the strategic architecture' and 'the engine' of the department; the AI conversation has matured into governance.

ACC (2026 CLO Survey): the CLO is now a business executive mandated to lead AI transformation while resource-starved; AI targets role evolution rather than headcount reduction; outside counsel remains the 'pressure valve' for regulatory surges - in tension with CLOC's framing.

Thomson Reuters Institute: the strategic-GC narrative is self-assessed (86% of GCs vs 17% of C-suite); legal must prove outcomes, not tasks; AFAs and formal panels have barely moved in a decade despite the AI pricing talk.

Gartner (Weston Wicks): the end state is business self-service and AI intake (60% of departments by 2029); multi-agent legal applications reduce reliance on external counsel; neither firms nor clients yet know how to price AI-assisted work.

Deloitte (US CLO Program; Tom Brunt, Deloitte Legal UK): AI is a structural force; hourly billing share expected to fall from 72% to 44%; 84% have not redesigned roles; move risk evaluation closer to where business occurs; view delivery through an ecosystem lens rather than inside vs outside.

Blickstein Group (Brad Blickstein): departments are ahead of their firms on AI but lack a strategy for what to demand from firms; fewer than one in five have pressed for AI savings; many legal ops leaders do not control AI tool selection.

Axiom (ALSP, interested party; Daniel Hayter, Chris Frickland): law firm panels are obsolete and should be replaced by per-matter talent/technology/price decisions; 80% will move work away from firms; only 7% have made AI work because the operating layer around the tools is the hard part.

Legal AI vendors (Daniel Lewis of LegalOn; Omar Haroun of Eudia): billable-hour incentives mean in-house teams, not law firms, will capture AI productivity; in-house needs are 'at odds with' law firm needs.

AI-native law firms (General Legal's JP Mohler; Crosby; Norm Law; Covenant): AI is the first reviewer, lawyers supervise like partners, pricing is fixed, only experienced lawyers are hired - no junior pyramid.

Skeptics: Above the Law and ABA Journal experts say AI is a convenient label for ordinary cost-cutting (Baker McKenzie) and law firm revenues are still booming; Forrester (via National Law Review) expects 25% of planned AI spend deferred to 2027; Mary O'Carroll notes new legal-engineering roles are hard to get headcount for; Juro data shows 84% of in-house lawyers see no fee reductions from firm AI use.

Practitioner (Gio DiLuca, Senior Director Legal Operations, Lowe's): the head of legal ops has moved from efficiency manager to strategic partner, platform architect, ecosystem orchestrator, executive storyteller and AI governance steward.
gaps: No neutral, survey-based current adoption figure for legal front door / intake portals / NDA self-service in 2025-2026; only Gartner's 2029 prediction (via secondary reprints), Juro's vendor survey (13% already running routine contracts without daily legal involvement) and vendor marketing.

CLOC 2026 State of the Industry full report is gated; no CLOC data retrieved on legal ops team size, reporting lines, or who specifically owns AI governance. CLOC Global Institute 2026 session-level content and CLOC Compass detail beyond launch facts not retrieved.

All gartner.com pages returned 403; Gartner statistics and Weston Wicks quotes come from secondary reprints (SMBtech, Lawyers Weekly AU, Bloomberg Law). The Gartner note 'Predicts 2026: AI and Agentic AI Will Enable Legal Self-Service' and the Dec 2025 release 'Only 20% of Legal Matters Sent to Outside Counsel Stay Within Budget Range' are known by title only.

ACC full 2026 CLO report is gated and the ACC newsroom page returned 403; the '62% regularly sought for strategic input (up from 43%)' figure comes from a Substack and is unverified. The ACC 2025 Law Department Management Benchmarking figure (median firms used fell from 14 to 10) is from a search snippet; no 2026 edition confirmed; nothing new found on the ACC Legal Operations Maturity Model.
Blickstein Group 2025 LDO Survey full report not retrieved; all figures are secondary (Legal.io citing Legaltech News), and the Brad Blickstein quote may be a paraphrase.
EY Law General Counsel Study: only the April 2025 edition was found (figures from search snippets); no 2026 edition located.

No hard data on law firm associate class reductions or partner-role restructuring; only commentary (Axios, Forbes, Lawyer Monthly) that could not be fetched. Baker McKenzie layoffs details are from search snippets, not fetched articles.

No survey evidence that legal ops specifically owns knowledge curation; only indirect signals (Deloitte centralized data repositories, Axiom's 66% running default-configured AI, vendor 'institutional knowledge capture' features).
No 2026 market sizing for managed legal services or law-firm subsidiaries; the latest ALSP sizing is Thomson Reuters' January 2025 report ($28.5B; captives $1.8B).

Several quotes were extracted through a summarizing fetch model rather than read verbatim (flagged 'EXTRACTED' in notes); they need a verbatim check against the live page before publication. Quotes read directly from PDFs (ACC Key Findings, Deloitte US predictions, TR LDO Index) are exact.

The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted after about 28 searches, so some planned searches (Gartner Dec 2025 release, Law.com Corporate Counsel coverage, LawNext) were replaced with direct fetches; Law.com article was paywalled.

research:ai-writing-tells.summary: The best current catalog is Wikipedia's "Signs of AI writing" (WikiProject AI Cleanup, revised 2026-09-21), backed by practitioner lists (tropes.fyi, Feb 2026; Rough at Sea's LLM-ism Dictionary, Aug 2026) and peer-reviewed work. Kobak et al. (Science Advances, July 2025) found at least 13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts were LLM-processed, with "delves" at 28 times expected frequency. Reinhart et al. (PNAS 2025) measured present-participial clauses at 2 to 5 times human rates, the evidence behind the "highlighting the importance of" tail. Russell et al. (ACL 2025) showed frequent LLM users detect AI text almost perfectly, citing vocabulary (53%) and sentence structure (36%) most. Vocabulary tells are fading ("delve" dropped sharply in 2025) while negative parallelism persists (The Atlantic, July 2026, secondary access only). The em dash is weak evidence of authorship (Twain exceeds most models) but a strong public trigger; Freeburg (arXiv, March 2026) measured 0 to 10.6 per 1,000 words across models against a human mean of 3.2, and OpenAI treated it as a defect (Nov 2025). Style authorities agree every em dash function has a more formal substitute. The notes file contains a five-group taxonomy with invented business-register rewrites, an em dash decision guide with six examples plus rules for en dashes, spaced hyphens and double hyphens, and a ranked view of which tells matter to expert readers: content emptiness first, manufactured-drama constructions second, template rhythm third, dashes fourth, vocabulary last. Wikipedia's warning frames everything: fix the underlying vagueness, not only the surface sign. Search budget ran out after 15 searches; several paywalled primaries were unreachable.

findings.claim: Wikipedia's 'Signs of AI writing' is the most complete, actively maintained catalog, and it warns that the signs are symptoms, not the problem to fix.
findings.detail: Living document by WikiProject AI Cleanup (project formed 2023); most recent revision observed 2026-09-21. Groups tells under Content (inflated significance, superficial '-ing' analyses, promotional tone, vague attribution, 'Despite its... challenges' conclusions), Language (AI vocabulary, copula avoidance such as 'serves as', negative parallelism in three subtypes, rule of three) and Style (title case, mechanical bold, inline bold-header lists, em dashes). It also cautions that not all text with these features is AI-written.
findings.source_title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing
findings.exact_quote: Please do not merely treat these signs as the problems to be fixed; that could just make detection harder.

findings.claim: AI vocabulary tells shift by model generation; 'delve' has largely receded, so word lists age quickly and density matters more than any single word.
findings.detail: Wikipedia's era table: 2023 to mid-2024 (GPT-4) includes delve, tapestry, testament, landscape, pivotal, crucial, underscore, intricate, interplay, vibrant; mid-2024 to mid-2025 (GPT-4o) includes align with, fostering, enhance, highlighting, showcasing; mid-2025 on (GPT-5) shrinks to emphasizing, enhance, highlighting, showcasing. The page says delve dropped off sharply in 2025.
findings.source_title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, section 'High density of AI vocabulary words'
findings.exact_quote: an edit (post-2022) introducing lots of them, lots of times, is one of the strongest tells for AI use

findings.claim: Peer-reviewed word-frequency analysis found at least 13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts were processed with LLMs, detected through excess 'style' words.
findings.detail: Kobak, Gonzalez-Marquez, Horvat and Lause analyzed over 15 million PubMed abstracts (2010 to 2024). Per arXiv v3: 454 excess words in 2024; unlike Covid-era excess words (content nouns), 2024's were mostly style words, 66% verbs and 14% adjectives. Frequency ratios: delves 28.0, underscores 13.8, showcasing 10.7; largest gaps among common words: potential, findings, crucial. Lower bound reaches 30 to 40% in some subcorpora. Science Advances page returned 403, so figures are from arXiv versions.
findings.source_title: Delving into LLM-assisted writing in biomedical publications through excess vocabulary
findings.exact_quote: at least 13.5% of 2024 abstracts were processed with LLMs

findings.claim: The present-participle tail and noun-heavy density are measurable: instruction-tuned LLMs use present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times the human rate.
findings.detail: Reinhart et al. applied Biber's feature set to GPT-4o and Llama 3 variants. GPT-4o: present participial clauses 5.3x human rate, nominalizations 2.1x, 'that' subject clauses 2.6x, phrasal coordination 1.9x, agentless passives about half. Overused words in GPT-4o by rate multiple: camaraderie 162, tapestry 155, intricate 119. Base Llama models were close to human rates; instruction tuning produced the divergence.
findings.source_title: Do LLMs write like humans? Variation in grammatical and rhetorical styles
findings.exact_quote: Instruction tuning appears to make the model output less human, not more

findings.claim: Frequent LLM users are near-perfect detectors of AI text, and the clues they cite most are vocabulary and sentence structure, followed by punctuation, originality, quotations, over-explanation, formatting and formula conclusions.
findings.detail: Russell, Karpinska and Iyyer (ACL 2025): 300 articles; majority vote of five expert annotators misclassified 1 of 300; non-experts were near chance (56.7% TPR). Clue shares: vocabulary 53.1%, sentence structure 35.9% (including lists of three), grammar and punctuation 24.8%, originality 23.7%, quotations 22.3%, clarity 19.5%, formatting 15.0% (balanced paragraphs, consistent headers), conclusions 13.1% (repetitive, optimistic). Non-experts wrongly flagged any formal or correct prose. Implies that Spaarke's complaining readers, likely heavy LLM users, are accurate judges.
findings.source_title: People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text
findings.exact_quote: quotes feel fake, every expert speaks the same way and it's too homogenous with the text

findings.claim: Em dash frequency is model-specific rather than universal: 0 to 10.6 per 1,000 words across twelve models, against a human essay mean of 3.23 with a 50-fold human range.
findings.detail: Freeburg (arXiv preprint, not evidently peer reviewed): GPT-4.1 10.62, Claude Opus 4.6 9.09, DeepSeek V3 6.95, Gemini 2.5 Pro 3.53, Llama 0.00. Human baseline from eight published essays (57,232 words): mean 3.23, range 0.33 to 17.12. Under suppression instructions GPT-4.1 stayed at 9.10 while Claude Opus fell to 0.19. Hypothesis: the em dash is markdown structure leaking into prose, shaped by fine-tuning.
findings.source_title: The Last Fingerprint: How Markdown Training Shapes LLM Prose
findings.exact_quote: the em dash is markdown leaking into prose

findings.claim: Wikipedia's em dash tell is about placement as well as frequency: models use em dashes where people would use commas, parentheses or colons, which maps directly onto a replacement guide.
findings.detail: The em dash section also notes that AI em dashes are often spaced, and cites an unidentified July 2026 study finding that among contemporary models only Claude exceeded professional writers' em dash rate while ChatGPT fell below it. The observation that humans more often use '(misused) hyphens and en dashes' explains why swapping glyphs can look superficially human but is still poor practice in formal publishing.
findings.source_title: Wikipedia:Signs of AI writing, section 'Overuse of em dashes'
findings.exact_quote: uses them in places where humans are more likely to use commas, parentheses, colons, or (misused) hyphens (-) and en dashes (–)

findings.claim: OpenAI publicly treated ChatGPT's em dash habit as a defect to fix, confirming the mark's status as a recognized tell.
findings.detail: On 2025-11-14 Sam Altman announced that ChatGPT now obeys custom instructions not to use em dashes. TechCrunch (Sarah Perez) reported the mark had become a telltale sign of AI text in school papers, emails and social posts. Default behavior without an instruction was unchanged.
findings.source_title: OpenAI says it's fixed ChatGPT's em dash problem
findings.exact_quote: If you tell ChatGPT not to use em-dashes in your custom instructions, it finally does what it's supposed to do!

findings.claim: Style authorities agree every em dash function has a more formal substitute: comma pair, parentheses, colon, semicolon or full stop.
findings.detail: The Punctuation Guide says the em dash replaces commas, parentheses or colons, is more emphatic than commas, less formal than parentheses and the colon, and should be limited to two per sentence. Chicago Manual of Style Q&A concedes that between two independent clauses 'a semicolon or a period might be better than a dash' and advises editing dashes out when in doubt. Wikipedia's Dash article documents the spaced en dash as British house style (Penguin, CUP, Routledge), the double hyphen as a typewriter proxy, and the en dash for closed numeric ranges.
findings.source_title: Em dash
findings.exact_quote: Dashes are considered less formal than parentheses; they are also more intrusive.

findings.claim: The em dash is weak evidence of authorship even though it is a strong trigger of suspicion; defenders note that canonical human prose matches or exceeds model rates.
findings.detail: SlopDetector (a detection vendor) counted 10.13 em dashes per 1,000 words in Huckleberry Finn and 8.12 in Moby-Dick versus GPT-4.1's 10.62, concluding the gap is 'much smaller and noisier than the myth suggests' and weighting the signal low. Brian Phillips in The Ringer (2025-08-20) argues models copied the mark from skilled human writers. The vendor blog describes Freeburg's paper as peer-reviewed; arXiv shows no such indication.
findings.source_title: Is the Em Dash an AI Tell? We Measured Dash Density Across Human vs AI Texts
findings.exact_quote: A dash is a keystroke, not a thought.

findings.claim: Negative parallelism ('it is not X, it is Y') is reported as the most durable AI tell, about three times more frequent in LLM text than human text, and is spreading into corporate filings.
findings.detail: Source is Will Oremus, The Atlantic, 2026-07-12, which could not be fetched. Wikipedia's 'Negative parallelism' article relies solely on it for the threefold figure. An aggregator summary reports a Barron's count of the construction in Fortune 500 filings rising from about 50 (2023) to over 200 (2025), a Washington Post dataset finding 'not just X, but Y' in about 6% of ChatGPT messages in one July, and that the pattern shows 'no signs of abating' unlike 'delve'. All figures need verification at source. Wikipedia's Signs page separately documents three subtypes.
findings.source_title: Negative parallelism (citing The Atlantic, 'The Most Famous AI Writing Tic Is Also the Most Mysterious')

findings.claim: The cause of overused vocabulary points to human-feedback training rather than architecture or training data, which explains why the tells read as 'trying to sound good'.
findings.detail: Juzek and Ward (COLING 2025) identified 21 focal words in scientific abstracts and found no evidence that architecture, algorithms or training data cause the overuse; model testing was consistent with RLHF. Their follow-up (BIAS 2025 workshop, 2025-08-03) showed experimentally with Llama that human raters systematically prefer text containing some overused words, and framed this as misalignment between annotation workers and end users. Competing accounts for the em dash: old digitized books (Goedecke, 2025-10-30) and markdown leakage (Freeburg).
findings.source_title: Why Does ChatGPT 'Delve' So Much? Exploring the Sources of Lexical Overrepresentation in Large Language Models
findings.exact_quote: We fail to find evidence that lexical overrepresentation is caused by model architecture, algorithm choices, or training data.

findings.claim: Practitioner catalogs cover the structural tells that lack academic measurement, and they stress that clustering and repetition, not single uses, give prose away.
findings.detail: tropes.fyi (launched Feb 2026) lists negative parallelism, em-dash addiction, 'The X? A Y.' self-answered questions, false ranges, short punchy fragments, 'Here's the kicker', 'Let's break this down', title case headings, bold-first bullets, fractal summaries, signposted conclusions and the tie-back. Rough at Sea's LLM-ism Dictionary (2026-08-15) adds the 'colon epiphany', 'suspiciously even paragraph lengths', paragraphs where 'Every thought receives a landing sentence', the 'conclusion echo' and the 'agency ending', and describes LLM prose as 'statistically well-behaved'.
findings.source_title: Tropes: AI Writing Pattern Directory
findings.exact_quote: Remember: any of these patterns used once might be fine. The problem is when multiple tropes appear together or when a single trope is used repeatedly.

findings.claim: AI-preferred vocabulary is entering human speech, so vocabulary-based judgments will increasingly misfire on human writers.
findings.detail: Yakura et al. (Max Planck Institute for Human Development and collaborators) analyzed 737,083 hours of podcast audio and ran a preregistered experiment with 496 participants; words such as delve, showcase, boast, intricacies and meticulous rose abruptly in natural speech after ChatGPT's release. Supports ranking vocabulary as the least durable tell.
findings.source_title: Empirical evidence of Large Language Model's influence on human spoken communication

findings.claim: In professional settings, perceived heavy AI assistance lowers perceived sincerity, which is the business cost of sounding like AI.
findings.detail: Cardon and Coman surveyed 1,100 full-time US professionals (International Journal of Business Communication, 2025). Over 80% rated supervisors as sincere when messages showed low AI assistance, versus 40 to 52% with high assistance. Journal page returned 403; details are from HR Dive's report. The study covers workplace messages, so it applies to published thought leadership only by analogy.
findings.source_title: Managers risk loss of trust by over-relying on AI-written messages, study finds

viewpoints: Tells are symptoms of generic, inflated, unsourced prose; scrubbing the surface signs without adding specifics only makes the text harder to flag and no better to read (Wikipedia WikiProject AI Cleanup).

The em dash is a legitimate mark that models learned from skilled human writers; treating it as a tell harms writers, and canonical prose (Twain, Melville) matches model rates (The Ringer, SlopDetector).
The em dash is measurably overused by specific models and functions as a fingerprint of fine-tuning choices; the vendor itself treated it as a defect (Freeburg 2026; Altman, Nov 2025).

Causes are disputed: digitized older books (Goedecke), human-feedback preference for certain words (Juzek and Ward), markdown leakage (Freeburg), post-training on reasoning tasks for negative parallelism (Salvaggio); The Atlantic reportedly calls the cause of negative parallelism unresolved.
The tells are a moving target: vocabulary lists shrink with each model generation and 'delve' has faded, while negative parallelism persists across all major models.
Humans are converging on model vocabulary (Yakura et al.) and non-expert readers misread any formal, correct prose as AI (Russell et al.), so false accusations against human writers will rise.

For expert professional readers the costliest tells are substantive (unsupported significance claims, vague attribution, conclusions that restate) and manufactured-drama constructions, with the em dash a cheap-to-fix trigger and vocabulary the least durable signal (researcher synthesis from the cited evidence).
gaps: The Atlantic article by Will Oremus (2026-07-12) could not be fetched; the threefold negative-parallelism figure, the Barron's Fortune 500 filing count and the Washington Post 6% figure come only via Wikipedia and an aggregator (aiweekly.co) and must be verified at source. The original measurer of the threefold figure was not identified.

Washington Post (2025-04-09), Rolling Stone, Marketplace (2026-08-24), Science Advances, PMC and Sage pages returned 403, captcha or paywall redirects; arXiv versions and trade-press reports were used instead.
Sam Kriss's New York Times Magazine essay (2025-12-03) was not read directly; only a Longreads notice and a weak secondary discussion were reachable.
The 'July 2026 study' that Wikipedia cites on em dash rates by model versus professional writers was not identified.
No quantitative study was found for colon reveals, one-sentence dramatic paragraphs, uniform paragraph length, title-case headings or bold lead-in bullets; these rest on practitioner catalogs only.
No study specific to legal-industry or general-counsel readers' reactions to AI-sounding thought leadership was found; the ranking of which tells matter most is inference from general evidence.
Juzek and Ward's list of 21 focal words was not retrieved. Kobak et al. figures come from arXiv v3 and may differ slightly from the Science Advances version.

The session-wide web search budget was exhausted after 15 searches in this track; later discovery relied on URLs already surfaced, so authoritative sources such as Garner, the Economist style guide or a CMOS statement on em dashes and AI were not located.
All quotations were retrieved through a summarizing fetch tool and should be checked verbatim against the live pages before publication.

research:knowledge-management-and-ai.summary: Across 2025-2026 sources, the legal industry's consensus framing is that AI is no longer the constraint; knowledge is. Conference programmes (Inside Practice AI x KM New York, April 2026; Inside Legal KM London, September 2026), named KM leaders (Oz Benamram, Tom Humberstone), trade press (Artificial Lawyer, Legal IT Insider, LawSites) and publishers (LexisNexis, Thomson Reuters) all describe KM shifting from maintaining repositories to orchestrating AI workflows, curating trusted content and assuring data quality. Hard numbers are thin and mostly vendor-sourced: iManage's 3,185-respondent benchmark (85% piloting AI, 17% embedded), Gartner's cross-industry 60% abandonment prediction for projects lacking AI-ready data, and Thomson Reuters data showing in-house gen-AI use (47%) now ahead of firms (41%) and 94% of professionals demanding grounding in authoritative content. Technical evidence: Stanford RegLab found RAG legal tools still hallucinate 17-33%; the Vals legal benchmark was built from law-firm-supplied ideal answers, showing work product becoming evaluation material; Anthropic's legal plugin takes the organization's playbook as its configuration. A notable gap supports the article's thesis: CLOC Core 12 and ACC Maturity Model 2.0 still define KM as human reuse of work product and never mention AI, and ACC's "advanced" bar is one full-time KM professional. I found no body that explicitly names legal operations as the knowledge curator. Risks are well documented: US v. Heppner (privilege), embeddings stripping ethical-wall permissions, notetaker transcripts and retention. Quotes came through a summarizing fetch tool and need re-verification; the search budget ran out before ILTACON 2026 coverage.

findings.claim: The dominant 2026 industry framing is that knowledge, not AI, is the bottleneck for legal AI.
findings.detail: Inside Practice built its April 29, 2026 'AI x KM: New York' programme around this line, with chief knowledge officers and KM directors from DLA Piper, Paul Hastings, McDermott, Fried Frank, McGuireWoods and Stradley Ronon speaking. Its September 17, 2026 London KM event page adds: 'The gap between AI potential and AI performance is overwhelmingly a knowledge management problem.' Event-organizer copy, so it reflects how the KM community is positioning itself.
findings.exact_quote: Artificial intelligence is no longer the bottleneck for law firms. Knowledge is.
findings.source_title: AI x KM: New York (event page)

findings.claim: Oz Benamram (SKILLS founder, now Pillsbury Chief AI Officer) says AI exposes poor KM and that clean, structured, context-rich KM becomes decisive.
findings.detail: In Artificial Lawyer's 2026 predictions, Benamram lists the contents of modern KM as precedents, outcomes and expertise signals under a 'Knowledge as a competitive weapon' heading. Same piece: Winston Weinberg (Harvey) 'In 2026, context wins' and Ed Walters (Clio) 'Out: Prompt engineering. In: Context engineering.' Quote wording returned identically on two fetches.
findings.exact_quote: Clean, structured, context-rich KM (precedents, outcomes, expertise signals) becomes decisive
findings.source_title: Artificial Lawyer Predictions 2026

findings.claim: The 2026 SKILLS Legal AI Survey (130 of the largest law firms) indicates firms have identified the knowledge-management layer as the next AI priority.
findings.detail: Benamram notes KM-layer tools (DeepJudge, Ask iManage) have among the highest 'Consider' scores, says RAG infrastructure and data governance will decide AI's long-term success, and that 'AI amplifies the cost of fragmentation.' Survey write-up was published on Harvey's blog on 2026-03-06 with the full dashboard on 2026-03-12; treat as vendor-hosted.
findings.exact_quote: Figuring out RAG infrastructure and data governance will be key to AI's long-term success
findings.source_title: 2026 SKILLS Legal AI Survey: Q&A With Oz Benamram

findings.claim: At ILTACON 2025 the KM roundtable described the KM role as shifting from maintaining knowledge bases to orchestrating AI workflows and ensuring data quality, possibly requiring more KM hiring.
findings.detail: Artificial Lawyer relayed Draftwise's notes of a 14-speaker KM roundtable (DLA Piper, Paul Hastings, Goodwin; NetDocuments, iManage, Upland). Also reported: 'POC fatigue' and firm knowledge 'scattered across OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams, and personal folders.' Second-hand reporting of a vendor's notes.
findings.exact_quote: KM professionals are shifting from maintaining knowledge bases to orchestrating AI workflows and ensuring data quality.
findings.source_title: ILTACon Day Two: AI + KM, The Hour, Human Capital

findings.claim: The in-house frameworks (CLOC Core 12 and ACC Legal Operations Maturity Model 2.0) still define KM as human reuse of work product and do not mention AI; ACC's 'advanced' stage requires only one full-time KM professional.
findings.detail: CLOC: 'Implement processes and standards to collect, structure, and organize knowledge to save time and improve outcomes.' ACC (PDF read directly) defines KM as capturing structured and tacit knowledge assets; early stage: 'may be getting advice on same topic repeatedly; no effort to consolidate legal work product so it can be repurposed'; advanced stage: 'Mechanisms and tools for curation' and 'At least one full-time dedicated KM professional'. The absence of AI in both is my observation from reading them, and is an opening for the article.
findings.exact_quote: The process of capturing, distributing, and effectively using both structured and tacit knowledge assets, from work products (such as legal memos) to understanding of an issue due to prior experience.
findings.source_title: ACC Legal Operations Maturity Model 2.0

findings.claim: Corporate legal departments now use generative AI more than law firms (47% vs 41% in 2026, up from 23% and 28%), and 94% of professionals demand AI grounded in authoritative content.
findings.detail: Thomson Reuters blog (Marjorie Richter) summarizing the 2026 AI in Professional Services Report and 2026 Future of Professionals Report. Also: 96% require confidential-data safeguards; 78% of corporate clients say AI-enabled quality improvements are essential but only 6% say providers deliver. Emerging roles expected: AI-specialist professionals 39%, AI implementation managers 33%, AI-specialist trainers 32%.
findings.source_title: What legal professionals say about the role of AI and law in 2026

findings.claim: iManage's 2026 benchmark found 85% of organizations piloting or using AI but only 17% embedding it in daily operations, attributing the gap to knowledge foundations.
findings.detail: n=3,185 decision-makers, 26 countries, fielded Sep-Oct 2025, across legal, accounting, financial services (not legal-only). Organizations with mature knowledge foundations were nearly twice as likely to report revenue growth; 72% plan new document/knowledge platform investment within two years; 30% had policy-impacting incidents from unsanctioned AI; 37 minutes a day spent searching. Vendor research from a DMS provider with an interest in the conclusion.
findings.exact_quote: AI success isn't about who experiments fastest—it's about who has done the foundational work.
findings.source_title: Organizations with Strong Knowledge Foundations Pull Ahead on AI, Growth, and Client Trust, New iManage Study Finds

findings.claim: Gartner predicts organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data through 2026; this is the closest available statistic for AI blocked by data quality, and it is cross-industry, not legal.
findings.detail: Same release: 63% of organizations do not have or are unsure they have the right data management practices for AI (Q3 2024 survey of 248 data management leaders). The Gartner page returned HTTP 403, so figures were read from the search-result snippet of the primary URL. No legal-specific equivalent was found.
findings.source_title: Lack of AI-Ready Data Puts AI Projects at Risk

findings.claim: RAG over curated legal content reduces but does not eliminate hallucination: leading legal research tools hallucinated 17-33% of the time, and curated, verified sources are the main mitigating factor.
findings.detail: Stanford RegLab/HAI study (Magesh, Surani, Dahl, Suzgun, Manning, Ho), arXiv May 2024 (outside the 2025-26 window; background). A 2026-02-19 literature review by Rebecca Fordon (AI Law Librarians) adds that general models hallucinated 58-88% on legal questions and that legal platforms do better because they search 'curated, verified legal databases with citators', yet 'roughly one in five responses contains errors'.
findings.exact_quote: Certain legal research providers have touted methods such as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as 'eliminating' or 'avoid[ing]' hallucinations
findings.source_title: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools

findings.claim: Finished legal work product is already being repurposed as AI evaluation material: the Vals Legal AI Report benchmark dataset was built from law firms' own questions, reference documents, ideal responses and correctness criteria.
findings.detail: Reed Smith, Fisher Phillips, McDermott Will & Emery, Ogletree Deakins and four anonymous firms contributed 500+ samples. This is concrete support for the thesis that knowledge now serves as gold-standard and evaluation material for AI, not only as a precedent for humans.
findings.exact_quote: The Consortium Firms together created the dataset used for the study and provided additional guidance and input that helped ensure the study best reflected real-world law firm work.
findings.source_title: Vals Legal AI Report (VLAIR)

findings.claim: The in-house playbook has become machine-readable configuration for AI agents: Anthropic's legal plugin (launched 2026-02-03) runs contract review against the organization's own playbook, and commentators see proprietary knowledge as the remaining differentiator.
findings.detail: Product page: the plugin is 'configurable to your organization's playbook'; the playbook is set 'in a local settings file to define standard positions, acceptable ranges, and escalation triggers.' Bob Ambrogi (LawSites, 2026-02-03) says incumbents' defence is 'proprietary datasets and subject-matter expertise'. Legal.io (2026-03-06) reports Thomson Reuters fell 18%, RELX 14%, Wolters Kluwer 13% after launch, and says for legal ops 'the near-term priority is governance rather than product evaluation.'
findings.exact_quote: the potent and powerful combination of proprietary datasets and subject-matter expertise
findings.source_title: Anthropic's Legal Plugin for Claude Cowork May Be the Opening Salvo...

findings.claim: Practitioners say the definition of a knowledge repository has widened beyond curated know-how to transactional and third-party content, and that AI magnifies data problems at scale.
findings.detail: Tiger Eye's 2026 KM trends piece quotes Tom Humberstone (Womble Bond Dickinson): 'GenAI is all about high quality knowledge to deliver value' and that repositories now 'encompass a broader set of sources'; Rob Taylor (Tiger Eye): 'AI will magnify any data issues you may have, and do so at pace, and at scale.'; Jenni Tellyn (3Kites) on need-to-know security: 'you have to work even harder at your knowledge management'. Also reports firms appointing senior knowledge leaders before buying technology. Legal IT Insider (2026-01-15) adds Jus Mundi's CEO: 'Firms with the best knowledge management will power the best AI skills.'
findings.exact_quote: knowledge repositories have evolved beyond traditional, curated know-how to encompass a broader set of sources now.
findings.source_title: Legal Knowledge Management Trends for 2026 and Beyond

findings.claim: 85% of corporate legal departments now have a dedicated AI resource or committee, but CLOC and Harbor frame legal ops' AI role as governance and operating model; neither explicitly assigns legal ops the knowledge-curator role.
findings.detail: Harbor/CLOC 2025 Law Department Survey (135 departments, median revenue USD 13bn; released 2025-12-08) and CLOC 2026 State of the Industry (2026-03-02): technology strategy a focus for 80%; only 32% expect lawyer headcount growth. No KM-specific metric is published. CLOC CEO Oyango Snell (2026-03-10) lists knowledge management among workflows where AI is being embedded.
findings.exact_quote: Legal operations has become the strategic lever that allows departments to close this productivity gap.
findings.source_title: CLOC Releases 2026 State of the Industry Report

findings.claim: Privilege, ethical walls and retention are live risks when knowledge is opened to AI: US v. Heppner held consumer-AI exchanges unprivileged; vector embeddings can strip DMS permission metadata; AI notetaker transcripts widen discovery and legal-hold exposure.
findings.detail: Heppner (S.D.N.Y., Rakoff J., bench ruling 2026-02-10, opinion 2026-02-17); Debevoise advises enterprise tools with confidentiality terms and documenting counsel's direction. Hintyr (vendor blog, 2026-03-27): 'Vector embeddings strip away the permission metadata that traditional document management systems rely on', citing CrowdStrike and a January 2026 Microsoft Copilot sensitivity-label advisory (not independently verified). Mayer Brown (2026-06-03) on notetakers: records 'may be accessed by individuals who were not present'.
findings.exact_quote: Because Claude is not an attorney…that alone disposes of Heppner's claim of privilege.
findings.source_title: SDNY Rules AI-Generated Documents Are Not Protected by Privilege

findings.claim: A sceptical counter-view holds that firms are buying AI without being able to measure impact, and that consultancy and vendor research in this area is methodologically opaque.
findings.detail: Stephen Embry (Above the Law, 2026-08-25) reviews Harbor's 2026 legal lab findings: law-firm technology spend up 41% from 2021-2025 to 5-6% of revenue, yet no firm had a mature impact-measurement framework. Embry questions sample size, participants and data sources. Relevant caution: most KM-and-AI statistics located in this research originate from DMS/KM vendors or consultancies.
findings.exact_quote: No participating firm in Harbor's 2026 legal lab reported having a mature framework for measuring AI's business impact.
findings.source_title: Law Firms Are Buying AI: But Are They Really Using It?

viewpoints: KM-as-foundation (dominant): AI is a commodity; curated, governed knowledge is the constraint and the differentiator (Inside Practice, Benamram, LexisNexis, iManage, Harvey, Tiger Eye, ClearPeople).
Context-over-content: what matters is situational context delivered to the model ('context engineering'), not the size of the precedent library (Weinberg of Harvey, Walters of Clio).

Sceptical/measurement view: firms and departments are buying AI but cannot show impact, and vendor or consultancy 'knowledge foundation' research is self-interested and methodologically thin (Embry, Above the Law).

Proprietary-data-moat view: incumbents' datasets and subject-matter expertise defend them against foundation-model entrants (Ambrogi), versus the market's reaction that the moat is weaker than assumed (publisher share-price falls after Anthropic's legal plugin).

Security-first view: opening knowledge to AI collides with ethical walls, privilege, need-to-know and retention, so KM must work harder rather than looser (Tellyn, Humberstone, Hintyr, Mayer Brown, Debevoise).

In-house governance view: legal operations' near-term AI job is governance and operating model (CLOC, Harbor, Legal.io); the in-house frameworks (Core 12, ACC) have not re-described KM for AI, and nobody yet names legal ops as knowledge curator.
RAG-is-not-enough view: even curated RAG legal tools err roughly one time in five, so human verification and evaluation sets persist (Stanford RegLab, AI Law Librarians).
gaps: ILTACON 2026 (August 2026) KM sessions and recaps: the session's web-search budget was exhausted before this search could run; nothing captured.

ILTA KM-specific survey data (KM headcount, KM budgets, KM teams leading AI programs): the ILTA 2025 Technology Survey executive summary contains no KM breakout; full results are members-only. No ILTA KM community or KM survey publication was reached.

No legal-specific statistic found for the share of AI projects blocked by poor knowledge or data quality; only Gartner's cross-industry 60% prediction (read via snippet because gartner.com returned 403) and unsourced event-marketing claims ('Taxonomy inconsistencies are the #1 AI deployment blocker').

No benchmark found for KM headcount, KM investment, or the proportion of KM teams formally leading AI programs at firms or in-house. The Totum Partners '20% Director KM salary increase' figure appears only on an event marketing page and was not verified.
SKILLS survey dashboard itself (skills.law) was not accessible; findings come from a Harvey-hosted write-up and interview. Harvey's exact relationship to the survey was not confirmed.
No source found in which CLOC, ACC or another body explicitly assigns legal operations the role of curating the department's knowledge for AI; this remains the article's own argument.

New knowledge sources: no neutral, citable source found describing billing narratives, decision logs and approvals, outside-counsel work product, intake Q&A, or expert corrections of AI output being managed as KM assets; only vendor marketing on redline-to-playbook conversion.
No 2025-26 primary source with data on 'legal knowledge engineer' or 'knowledge engineer' roles; the ABA Law Technology Today piece on legal engineers returned 403.
No evidence found of law departments or firms fine-tuning models on their own KM corpus as a mainstream practice.

Thomson Reuters Institute KM-specific commentary, Wolters Kluwer KM-specific findings, and any 3 Geeks and a Law Blog or LawNext 2025-26 KM-specific feature were not located. Wolters Kluwer, ACC resource library, ABA, Global Legal Post, White & Case and Clio pages blocked automated fetch; Harbor pages rendered empty.
ACC Legal Operations Maturity Model 2.0 PDF carries no publication date; release year not confirmed in this session.
