(3) Tso (senior associate, Clifford Chance; AL Jan 5, 2026): 'just-in-time, disposable software' confirmed, but the maintenance line is him conceding the traditional case before arguing the economics have shifted: "Traditionally, the argument for buying is totally fair: software needs maintenance, security, support, and it has to scale." Quoting it without 'Traditionally' misrepresents his position. (4) Linklaters (James Phoenix time-recording tool) and Debevoise (AI policy training game) are not in either AL article; they are in Paul Giedraitis's ILTA Peer to Peer piece on Above the Law, June 25, 2026. (5) The Bloomberg Law June 25, 2026 Ropes & Gray CIO quote could not be located and is unverified.
verdicts.corrected_detail: Exact quote: "Vibe-coding is a catalyst for change: it lets domain experts (e.g. lawyers) demonstrate ideas rather than just describe them, validate concepts before investing in full development..." Linklaters/Debevoise source: https://abovethelaw.com/2026/06/people-prompts-and-product-the-vibe-coding-revolution-in-biglaw/ (2026-06-25). Ropes & Gray quote unverified.

verdicts.claim: Serious risk commentary clusters on six points: MCP protocol attack classes, privilege, attribution, maintainability of AI-generated code, shadow AI, and default-on vendor agents without an admin off-switch.
verdicts.note: Legal Wire (Nicola Taljaard, Aug 3, 2026) confirms the five attack classes and CVE-2025-49596 at CVSS 9.4. But the 'exact quote' is a compression, not verbatim. MCP primary sources (2026-07-28 changelog and release blog) confirm authorization hardening: RFC 9207 iss validation, issuer-bound client credentials, DCR deprecated in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents. The spec does not 'add' Enterprise Managed Authorization: EMA is a pre-existing extension (SEP-990); the release blog only says the extensions framework is formalised "with Tasks joining other extensions, such as MCP Apps and Enterprise Managed Authorization (EMA)". Legal Wire does not mention EMA and relays SecurityWeek that the new version "shifts critical security responsibilities from the protocol itself to developers and platform operators" — a counterpoint to 'hardens'. BCG 54% and Clio 44% confirmed verbatim in the ATL/ILTA Peer to Peer article (Paul Giedraitis, June 25, 2026), both second-hand there (BCG 2025 global study via Law Practice Magazine; Clio 2025 Legal Trends Report). Microsoft MC1388706 confirmed via a Message Center mirror: published June 12, 2026, updated Aug 24, 2026; "enabled by default for tenants enrolled in Frontier"; "no dedicated admin or user toggle"; GA "early October 2026 (previously early September)". Scope caveat: default-on applies to Frontier-enrolled tenants and access is governed by Frontier enrollment plus Copilot licensing. US v. Heppner not checked. The 'six points' framing is the researcher's synthesis.
verdicts.corrected_detail: Exact Legal Wire quote: "The protocol layer disappears into the substrate, and the products above it get sorted by whether they added value the substrate could not commodify." Replace 'adds Enterprise Managed Authorization' with 'formalises an extensions framework that includes the existing Enterprise Managed Authorization extension'. MCP primary: https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28/ (2026-07-28). Microsoft mirror: https://mc.merill.net/message/MC1388706.

verdicts.claim: Openness at the data layer is coinciding with new lock-in at the AI-platform layer: playbooks, escalation chains, and house style are being encoded inside one frontier vendor's plugin and skill format.
verdicts.note: Artificial Lawyer Sep 18, 2026, verbatim: "As noted above all of this means that once you move your work into Astra, you will find it easier to stay there." ComplexDiscovery May 13, 2026 confirmed and stronger than the finding states: "A team that spends a quarter teaching a plugin its house style, its fallback clauses, its escalation thresholds, and its risk tolerances is building institutional knowledge inside the model — not inside a vendor's product. That cuts both ways. It deepens the lock-in to Claude." Joe Patrice's token/consumption-cost concern confirmed in the Sep 1 ATL piece. The thesis sentence itself is the researcher's synthesis of these sources; all three are trade-press opinion, not data. Best single citation for the lock-in point is the ComplexDiscovery sentence: https://complexdiscovery.com/claude-for-legal-arrives-and-the-legal-ai-stack-gets-re-segmented-overnight/

verdicts.claim: CLOC's 2026 State of the Industry report shows the conditions driving demand for control (80% prioritize technology strategy; 85% have dedicated AI oversight; expected outside-counsel spend increases fell from 58% to 37%), but CLOC made no explicit statement that vendors must be open.
verdicts.note: Read CLOC's release (March 2, 2026): 135 law departments, median revenue $13 billion, based on the 2025 Harbor Law Department Survey. Verbatim: "85% of legal departments now have dedicated AI oversight or resources"; "Only 37% of departments expect outside counsel spend to increase, down sharply from 58% last year"; priorities "technology strategy (80%), financial management (72%), and outside counsel and vendor management (62%)". Snell quote exact (Oyango Snell, President & CEO). LII's CGI report (Toby Weston, May 15, 2026) confirmed: "The era of the point solution is ending. The race to become the operating system for legal departments is underway" is the author's own synthesis of vendor announcements, correctly attributed to LII in the finding; Snell: "The AI conversation has matured. Teams are now sharing what has worked, what broke, and how they are governing it." No CLOC statement on vendor openness was seen in either source, consistent with the claim. 'Conditions driving demand for control' is the researcher's inference, not CLOC's language. The 85% is 'oversight or resources', slightly broader than 'oversight'.

verdicts.claim: Google Cloud launched Gemini Enterprise for Legal in preview on 2026-08-25 with MCP integrations to eleven legal platforms, making three frontier AI vendors with near-identical legal connector rosters within roughly four months.
verdicts.note: Read Google Cloud's press release (Aug 25, 2026): preview; eleven MCP integrations exactly as listed (Courtroom5, Docusign, Everlaw, Free Law Project's CourtListener, Harvey, iManage, Legora, NetDocuments, RelativityOne, Solve Intelligence, Thomson Reuters); customers Cleary, Freshfields, Weil, Williams & Connolly; integrators include Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, Eudia, Factor Law (plus Devoteam, Tribe AI, Valtech, Zazmic, Zencore, 66degrees). No Mitratech, Onit, Icertis, Agiloft or LexisNexis. Timing: May 12 to Sep 17 is four months and five days, so 'roughly four months' holds. 'Near-identical rosters' is interpretive: overlap on DMS, e-discovery, Harvey/Legora, TR and Docusign is real, but the counts differ (Anthropic 20+, Google 11, OpenAI 26) and each has names the others lack; 'heavily overlapping' is safer.

verify:open-platforms-api-mcp-build.overall_note:
Method and limits: the session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (0 of 200 left), so every check was done by WebFetch of the cited URL plus primary sources I could reach through site archive pages and PR Newswire organisation pages. All 15 cited URLs loaded. WebFetch answers come through a summarising model, so I re-queried for verbatim text wherever a quote mattered. Notes written to C:/Users/RALPHS~1/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/c--code-files-spaarke-website/aa6b682a-4844-485c-99e0-cb2228b928c3/scratchpad/research/open-platforms-api-mcp-build.verified.md. No repository files were touched.

Result: 7 confirmed, 8 corrected, 0 refuted. The research is substantively sound; dates, counts and product names held up almost everywhere. The errors are concentrated in quotes and attributions, which is exactly where a published piece gets caught.

Must-fix before publication:
1. Thomson Reuters: the 'Wherever lawyers are working...' quote is from the May 12 release (Joel Hron, CTO), not the Aug 20 release cited; the AWS product is Amazon Quick, not Amazon Q; the Claude Agent SDK underpins next-gen CoCounsel Legal, not the MCP connector.
2. Mark Pike is misquoted. Actual: "I partner with Claude to tackle certain projects that involve coding, but I am not the one coding."
3. The Legal Wire 'exact quote' is a compression. Actual: "The protocol layer disappears into the substrate, and the products above it get sorted by whether they added value the substrate could not commodify."
4. The Vibecode-Law quote drops "(e.g. lawyers)" without an ellipsis.
5. Jamie Tso's maintenance line begins "Traditionally, the argument for buying is totally fair:" — he is conceding the old argument before rebutting it; quoting the tail alone flips his stance.
6. 'Data problems wearing a model costume' is Joe Patrice paraphrasing HIKE2, not a direct quote.
7. Neil Cameron is the author of the LII iManage piece, not a quoted analyst.
8. MCP 2026-07-28 does not 'add' Enterprise Managed Authorization; EMA is a pre-existing extension (SEP-990). Authorization hardening itself is confirmed from the primary spec.
9. ILTACON 2026 was late August (Google's Aug 25 launch happened during it), not early September.

'Read-only' is asserted for both iManage's MCP Server and Brightflag's connector, and I could not find that term in any of the four pages checked. Since the article's argument likely turns on the read vs write distinction, do not describe either as read-only without a source.

Still unverified: Bloomberg Law June 25 Ropes & Gray CIO quote; Oddr MCP server; Legora-Intapp time write-back; Everlaw 'read access / system of record'; Mitratech ARIES 'proprietary AI ecosystem'; 'selected US firms' for Astra (source says 'selected firms'); 'deep legal research first' for TR; 'builders primarily in-house lawyers' for Vibecode-Law; US v. Heppner. OpenAI's primary page was 403 for me too, so Astra rests on two trade outlets that disagree on one number (LII: nine community plugins with 47 skills; Artificial Lawyer: 47 community plugins).

Extra context found along the way: Relativity announced RelativityOne was renamed Relativity aiR on Sep 16, 2026 and an OpenAI MCP integration on Sep 17, so 'RelativityOne' is already a dated product name. Docusign's Sep 30 date is still in the future as of today.

research:consulting-voice-and-tone.summary: I read 29 pages in full text (official HBR, strategy+business, and MIT SMR guidance; Barbara Minto's site; 11 HBR, 4 Deloitte Insights, 2 Bain, 3 MIT SMR, and 2 strategy+business articles, many on legal, AI, operations, and risk) and produced a notes file with 26 teachable traits, each with a verified quote of 30 words or fewer, URL, and date. Every quotation was machine-checked against downloaded source text. Core register: thesis within about 250 words, SCQA introductions, counted parallel frameworks, message-bearing headings, 15 to 25 word average sentences broken by short declaratives, 50 to 80 word paragraphs, inline-attributed statistics with sample and date, numbers interpreted skeptically, named and quantified one-paragraph cases, one calibrated hedge per claim, "we" and "you," parenthetical exhibit references, and endings on consequence rather than summary. Em dashes: all these publications use them (0 to 11 per 1,000 words, typically 2 to 7), but one September 2026 HBR article uses none and stays fully in register. The notes show four dash "jobs" and rewrite real sentences with colons, parentheses, semicolons, commas, or two sentences. Also covered: what the publications avoid, eight opening patterns, and tone versus marketing and academic prose. Major limit: mckinsey.com refused automated access, so there are no verbatim McKinsey quotes; McKinsey conventions are flagged as unverified prior knowledge. BCG was read only through a summarizer. The session search budget ran out after 9 searches. Helper scripts and downloaded pages sit in the scratchpad research/raw folder.

findings.claim: HBR's official contributor guidelines define the target reader and explicitly reject unsurprising, promotional, and LLM-replicable ideas.
findings.detail: Guidelines signed by Amy Bernstein and Maureen Hoch list five qualities: expertise, evidence, originality, usefulness, good writing. Readers are described as "smart, skeptical, and busy." The most common rejection reason is unsurprising findings. HBR refuses pieces that come across as promotional. The seven pitch questions work as a pre-draft checklist. For an AI drafting workflow the implication is that voice alone is insufficient; original evidence and point of view must be supplied.
findings.exact_quote: The ideas should not be easily replicable by simply asking a large language model (LLM).
findings.source_title: Harvard Business Review's Guidelines for Contributors

findings.claim: strategy+business gives the most compact official definition of the register: clear, accessible, jargon-free, with intelligence, wit, and perspective; it declines promotional or narrowly functional pieces.
findings.detail: Writers' guidelines specify 500 to 3,500 words, a strategic (long-term, enterprise-level) frame, and readers who are thoughtful, pragmatic, and open to ideas beyond conventional wisdom. It declines articles that primarily market a product, consulting practice, or service, or that have a narrow functional focus. For legal operations this means tying tactics to enterprise outcomes. Page is undated (footer copyright 2026 PwC).
findings.exact_quote: We seek clear, accessibly written articles that avoid jargon and approach readers with intelligence, wit, and perspective.
findings.source_title: Writers' Guidelines

findings.claim: MIT SMR's editorial director states the balance of rigor and utility, and explains endnotes as a credibility signal for practitioners; the MIT SMR author guidelines page is now a closure notice.
findings.detail: Lisa Burrell's 2019 editor's letter names three criteria: ideas for a digital world, evidence-based thinking (lab experiments, field studies, data analysis, deep industry experience, synthesis), and accessible frameworks. The authors page (updated 2026-09-09, https://sloanreview.mit.edu/authors/) now states that print publication ceases after the fall issue, regular digital content continues through November 2026, and a new digital publication launches this winter, so detailed author guidance is no longer retrievable from the primary page.
findings.exact_quote: Rigor is necessary but not sufficient. Our readers are busy, and they seek utility.
findings.source_title: What We Publish, and Why

findings.claim: The Pyramid Principle's primary statement is a single sentence; SCQA, answer-first, MECE grouping, and action titles are the working rules taught around it, and published articles apply them in softened form.
findings.detail: Minto's own site names the introduction device the "Situation, Complication, Question Framework" for identifying the question in the reader's mind. Secondary consulting sources (Tom Spencer blog 2021-06-21; Management Consulted 2022-09-20; Slideworks 2023-09-20, ex-McKinsey and ex-BCG authors) add: answer first, group and summarize, order logically, MECE, and action titles under 15 words that state the takeaway so a reader of headings alone gets the argument. In the article corpus this appears as a thesis within about 250 words, message-bearing headings, and full-sentence exhibit captions (Bain 2019 caption: "Many AI uses by legal groups have already been proven").
findings.exact_quote: The Minto Pyramid Principle says that your thinking will be easy for a reader to grasp if you present the ideas organized as a pyramid under a single point.
findings.source_title: Minto Pyramid Principle Concept

findings.claim: Em dashes are universal in these publications but not essential to the register: density ranged from 0 to 11 per 1,000 words across 16 articles, and a September 2026 HBR article of 1,756 words contains none.
findings.detail: Researcher's automated counts: MIT SMR column 11.0 per 1,000 words; HBR pieces 2.6 to 8.4; Deloitte 1.7 to 5.8; Bain 2019 legal article 1.4; s+b 6.2; HBR 'True Cost of Corporate Scandals' 0.0. Official guideline pages of HBR, MIT SMR, and s+b also use them. HBR magazine, Deloitte, Bain, and s+b set the dash closed; MIT SMR and older HBR digital posts set it spaced (AP style). The zero-dash HBR article relies on colons, commas, and short sentences, for example: "People are watching. And when they do not like what they see, they walk."
findings.exact_quote: People are watching. And when they do not like what they see, they walk.
findings.source_title: Research: The True Cost of Corporate Scandals? Talent.

findings.claim: The em dash does four jobs in this genre (paired aside, inserted list, end-of-sentence punch, trailing elaboration), and each has a clean substitute: parentheses, colon, period or semicolon, or comma plus reduced clause.
findings.detail: The notes rewrite nine real sentences. Example: the quoted HBR sentence becomes "If they cannot complete it, they do not have a transformation project. They have a technology experiment." Another: "Their prescription for incumbents is exactly right: rearchitect before you automate." Two-sentence rewrites are usually stronger because they create the short declarative the genre favors. Warning recorded: do not swap every dash for a comma, which produces run-ons; identify the job first. The colon is the natural workhorse (20 colons in 2,376 words in the same HBR article) and semicolons remain in active use in HBR and Bain.
findings.exact_quote: If they cannot complete it, they do not have a transformation project—only a technology experiment.
findings.source_title: Stop Automating Old Processes. Design New Ones Instead.

findings.claim: Statistics are attributed inline with source, instrument, sample, and date in the same sentence, and are usually given a comparison (base, peer, or before and after).
findings.detail: No orphan percentages were found in the corpus. HBR, Deloitte, Bain, BCG, and s+b use numerals with the % sign; MIT SMR and Deloitte spell out a number that starts a sentence. Bain's 2019 legal article pairs legal's 20% to 25% AI adoption with 40% in finance and 54% in HR. Method is disclosed in one or two plain sentences early (HBR 2026-09-21: "Our final sample covers 735 of the largest U.S. public companies over eight years").
findings.exact_quote: BCG’s January 2026 “AI Radar,” surveying 640 CEOs across 16 markets, reports that corporations expect to roughly double AI spending this year, from 0.8% of revenue to about 1.7%.
findings.source_title: Stop Automating Old Processes. Design New Ones Instead.

findings.claim: The register earns trust by telling the reader what a number does and does not prove, and by conceding the best objection once.
findings.detail: After citing Wayfair's 2.5 million corrected tags and 41,000 automated tickets per month, the HBR authors immediately limit the claim. Bain's 2019 legal article uses the classic one-sentence concession: "To be sure, AI still gets a lot of hype from vendors and the technology media, but plenty of cases have delivered substantial business value". This measured move is the clearest separator from marketing copy.
findings.exact_quote: Those figures demonstrate the scale of the redesigned workflow, not by themselves its business value
findings.source_title: Stop Automating Old Processes. Design New Ones Instead.

findings.claim: Examples are named, quantified, one paragraph long, and built on three beats (situation, action, measured result); when a client cannot be named, the anonymization is specific about sector, region, and scale.
findings.detail: Bain's legal department article gives JPMorgan (360,000 hours of review cut), Coca-Cola, and Liberty Mutual cases, each in a single paragraph introduced with 'for instance' or 'Consider'. Deloitte's anonymized form: "a leading European telecommunications provider consolidated four separate knowledge silos serving 19 million customers". HBR pairs a failure case with a success case and states exactly what differs (Deloitte Australia versus Wayfair).
findings.exact_quote: Coca-Cola launched a self-service portal that reduced contract-drafting time for many matters from up to 10 hours to around 15 minutes.
findings.source_title: Corporate Legal Eagles Start to Embrace Artificial Intelligence

findings.claim: Headings carry a message or instruction rather than a topic, with three house variants plus a new AI-search variant.
findings.detail: HBR: title case tied to the framework ("Decision 2: Decide Where Human Authority Remains"). Deloitte: sentence case message phrases. Bain 2019: sentence-case gerund phrases ("Turning digital hype into practical reality"), with bold run-in imperatives inside sections ("Think big."). Bain 2026 (https://www.bain.com/insights/how-to-architect-for-agentic-ai/, 2026-05-29) uses question headings answered by a first sentence that restates the question, which reads as formatted for AI retrieval and is more repetitive for human readers. No article uses headings called Introduction or Conclusion.
findings.exact_quote: Start with capabilities, not channels
findings.source_title: The next tech infrastructure advantage is intelligence orchestration

findings.claim: There are two hedging dialects: HBR authors commit and limit scope precisely, while firm-published research (Deloitte especially) hedges densely with could, may, and appears to.
findings.detail: HBR example: "Our research suggests that assumption is wrong." (2026-09-21). Deloitte's honest-scope model is worth copying: "The scenarios that follow are plausible depictions of future states, not forecasts." (2026-09-09). But Deloitte's "organizations could be up to 88 times more likely" is both hedged and extravagant. Recommendation in the notes: one hedge per claim, placed on the verb, never stacked; prefer the HBR dialect for Spaarke and borrow from firms only exhibit discipline, method disclosure, and message headings.
findings.exact_quote: Taken together, these patterns suggest that AI-driven business outcomes peak when decision rights are distributed among complementary leaders.
findings.source_title: How the right mix of C-suite leadership can drive outsized AI returns

findings.claim: Articles end on consequence, not summary: a short final section that returns to the opening frame, often a contrasted pair of futures and a last sentence under 20 words.
findings.detail: HBR marks the turn with a typographic break instead of a heading; Deloitte uses a forward-looking heading. Other closers: MIT SMR 2026-03-30 "Let the machine do the lifting, not the leading."; Deloitte 2026-09-09 "In a future crowded with agents, speed to market will matter, but not as much as trust, governance, and human capabilities." Sections likewise close on a compact takeaway ("It is to be deliberate everywhere."). Many pieces also hand the reader a tool before leaving: diagnostic questions, a checklist, or a fill-in sentence.
findings.exact_quote: Companies that do that will create better work. Those that do not will simply produce faster messes.
findings.source_title: Stop Automating Old Processes. Design New Ones Instead.

findings.claim: Eight opening patterns recur; the most reusable for a general counsel audience is 'received view, then reversal' backed by the author's own evidence.
findings.detail: Patterns documented with quotes: data tension (HBR 2026-09-14); received view then reversal (HBR 2026-09-21, reversal line "Our research suggests that assumption is wrong."); named scene (HBR 2026-09-17); second-person provocation (HBR 2004-12, "Your company’s legal department is broken."); big number plus boardroom question (Deloitte 2026-06-17); classic SCQA (HBR 2012-07, turn sentence "That close relationship is being disrupted."); neglected relationship (HBR 2016-07-25); plain question (Deloitte 2025-12-17). All deliver the thesis within roughly 250 words.
findings.exact_quote: The traditional way companies think about regulatory penalties is almost entirely financial.
findings.source_title: Research: The True Cost of Corporate Scandals? Talent.

findings.claim: Measured rhythm: average sentence length of about 15 to 25 words in 14 of 16 articles, 10 to 25 percent of HBR sentences at eight words or fewer, and paragraphs averaging 50 to 80 words; practice is less austere than writing-coach advice.
findings.detail: Researcher's automated counts (regex sentence splitting, approximate). Exceptions: Heineman's 2016 HBR essay averages about 30 words per sentence and is the stiffest prose in the sample; the MIT SMR panel report is inflated by long quotations. Paragraph means: Deloitte 50 to 61, Bain 2019 77, s+b 69, MIT SMR column 54. HBR paragraph lengths could not be measured. Coaches quoted in HBR (Garner, Bernoff) urge short sentences, yet every article carried sentences of 30 or more words; the real discipline is variation and one idea per sentence.
findings.exact_quote: The goal of the 4A framework is not to be conservative everywhere. It is to be deliberate everywhere.
findings.source_title: Stop Automating Old Processes. Design New Ones Instead.

findings.claim: Legal-trained writers must invert their habitual structure, and practitioners explicitly treat McKinsey Quarterly as a style model.
findings.detail: HBR's 2014 business-writing guide profiles a Harvard Law graduate who joined McKinsey and was told to get to the point faster: legal and academic writing builds to the conclusion, business writing starts with it. A second profiled consultant "began reading business publications, like McKinsey Quarterly, for style." Bryan Garner, quoted in the same piece: "One of the great diseases of business writing is postponing the message to the middle part of the writing". He also advises contractions, verbs over -ion nouns, and a buzzword blacklist (actionable, core competency, impactful, incentivize).
findings.exact_quote: But in business communications, it’s best to start with your conclusion first.
findings.source_title: How to Improve Your Business Writing

viewpoints: Answer first (Minto, Garner, consulting training) versus narrative hook (HBR features often spend two or three paragraphs on a scene or tension first). Both reach the thesis within about 250 words; a recorded critique of answer-first is that readers who reject the headline claim may skip the support.

Austere coaching advice (short sentences, simple words) versus actual published practice (about 20 words per sentence on average, with regular 30-plus word sentences). The working discipline is variation and one idea per sentence, not brevity as such.

Commitment versus caution: HBR academic and practitioner authors state findings flatly and scope them precisely; consulting-firm research, Deloitte above all, wraps similar claims in could, may, and appears to, which reads as legal caution.
Em dashes are universal in these outlets but dispensable: density varies from 0 to 11 per 1,000 words inside the same publication family, and a zero-dash 2026 HBR article reads fully in register.

Headings for human readers (message phrases, imperatives) versus headings for machine retrieval (Bain 2026 question headings with answer-first sentences that restate the question). The latter is efficient for AI search and more repetitive to read.

The corrective 'not X, but Y' frame is a hallmark of HBR argument and also a widely recognized marker of machine-written prose in 2026. The publications earn it by attributing X to a real, named belief; the researcher recommends a cap for the drafting agent (own recommendation, not sourced).

HBR's 2026 guidelines hold that ideas an LLM could produce unaided are not publishable, which implies voice imitation alone will not place an article in this genre; original data, cases, and point of view must be supplied by Spaarke.

Two dialects inside the register: warm, direct, second-person HBR and MIT SMR author pieces versus cooler, third-person, bulleted, survey-heavy firm research. The researcher recommends the HBR dialect for a small company addressing expert practitioners.
gaps: No McKinsey primary text: mckinsey.com timed out on four fetch-tool requests, one direct download never connected, and one public reader-proxy attempt returned an explicit 403 Access Denied, after which I stopped. No McKinsey Insights or McKinsey Quarterly article and no McKinsey Publishing editorial statement was read. The brief's request for McKinsey articles is unmet; the corpus is 11 HBR, 4 Deloitte, 2 Bain, 3 MIT SMR, 2 strategy+business. McKinsey conventions mentioned in the notes (spelled-out 'percent', '(Exhibit 1)' references) are from prior knowledge and need a human spot check in a browser.

BCG: one article read only through the fetch tool's summarizer (bcg.com returned 403 to direct download). BCG quotations, including the '(See Exhibit 1.)' form, are unverified; the summarizer's offered em-dash example contained no em dash, so its verbatim reliability is doubtful.

MIT SMR detailed author guidelines (length, article types, tone rules) are no longer on the primary page, which now carries a closure notice dated 2026-09-09; the support-site copy redirects to a login and was not pursued.

No interview or essay by a McKinsey or HBR editor analyzing house prose style was found before the shared session search budget (200 calls) ran out; only 9 of my searches executed. The editor and coach strand rests on three HBR business-writing articles (Birchard 2021, Bernoff 2016, O'Hara 2014) and ex-consultant secondary sources.

Barbara Minto's book was not consulted; her site provides only the one-sentence principle, and SCQA and MECE details come from secondary sources (Tom Spencer blog, Management Consulted, Slideworks, ModelThinkers via summarizer).

HBR paragraph lengths could not be measured because article text was available only as one unbroken block in page structured data; sentence statistics across the corpus are approximate (regex splitting, headings and table text mixed into HBR blocks).
Undated or partially dated sources: strategy+business writers' guidelines (copyright 2026 only), barbaraminto.com, ModelThinkers, and the Avery Content post (shows 'Sep 27' without a year).
No public style guide was found for Deloitte Insights, Bain, or BCG.

Process disclosure: besides the notes file, I wrote helper scripts and downloaded page copies to the session scratchpad at research/raw (not in any git repository) so that all 100-plus quotations could be machine-verified against source text. No repository file was modified.

verdicts.claim: The platform is defined as decision-centric: each operational decision comprises data, logic, action and security, integrated in one system.
verdicts.note: Seen on the docs page. Quote exact ('decisions' italicised). All four component definitions seen verbatim. The 2026-04-28 blog 'Connecting Agents to Decisions' carries the same four definitions; its headline sentence differs slightly: 'The Ontology is a system designed to represent the decisions in an enterprise, not simply the data.' The 'supersedes the semantic/kinetic/dynamic framing' remark is interpretation; the docs overview page still uses semantic/kinetic wording.

verdicts.claim: Palantir's own line between an operational platform and an analytical one is closing the action loop.
verdicts.note: Quote exact on the docs page. 'requires a different architecture than a classical database management solution optimized for reporting and analytics' seen. 'golden tables that flatten the richness of operations into narrow schemas' seen in the 2026-04-28 blog (not in the docs page).

verdicts.claim: Palantir explicitly rejects the label 'semantic layer' for its system.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. Language / Engine / Toolchain grouping, 'semantics must be paired with kinetics', nouns/verbs metaphor and Change Data Capture mention all seen. The sub-claim that Cognizant partner material still calls it a semantic layer was not checked (no URL, search unavailable) and should be treated as unverified.

verdicts.claim: The three-layer wording (semantic, kinetic, dynamic) comes from product marketing pages; the cleanest primary mapping is semantic = data, kinetic = action, dynamic = logic.
verdicts.note: Foundry product page sentence 'It integrates the semantic, kinetic, and dynamic elements of your business' seen (rendered page). Docs overview sentence on semantic elements (objects, properties, links) and kinetic elements (actions, functions, dynamic security) as a digital twin seen verbatim. But the exact_quote attributed to the AIP page was NOT found there on 2026-09-21: 'semantic data', 'kinetic action' and 'full power' are all absent from the rendered page, and also absent from /platforms/ontology/ and /docs/foundry/aip/overview. The semantic=data / kinetic=action / dynamic=logic mapping therefore rests on a quote I could not locate.
verdicts.corrected_detail: Do not cite the 'semantic data, dynamic logic, and kinetic action' quote to https://www.palantir.com/platforms/aip/ ; it is not on that page as currently published. Safe primary cites: Foundry page for the three adjectives; https://www.palantir.com/docs/foundry/ontology/overview for semantic vs kinetic elements. The three-way mapping is unverified.

verdicts.claim: Decisions are captured as first-class data through an action log and end-to-end decision lineage, then fed back for learning.
verdicts.note: Action log quote exact; 'What decision was made, by whom, when, and in what context?' seen. Why-ontology page: decision lineage sentence (when made, atop which version of enterprise data, through which application) and the training-data / prompting-principles sentence both seen verbatim. The sub-detail that use-case docs describe 'capturing decisions as data' as closing the operational loop was not found on the use-case pages I checked; treat that phrase as unverified.

verdicts.claim: Actions are governed transactions with rules, validations, side effects and write-back to source systems; the platform binds to existing systems rather than replacing them.
verdicts.note: Webhooks page: Salesforce / SAP / any HTTP server sentence seen; writeback-runs-first-and-failure-blocks-changes sentence seen. verdicts.corrected_detail: The 47% GenAI-access figure is cited by the report from TR Institute's 2026 AI in Professional Services Report (Feb 2026), not from the GC interviews. The 'Decision-making using analytics' 19% felt / 39% anticipated figures (Figure 15) are, per the report's own text, 'data from the Thomson Reuters Future of Professionals Report 2025' (June 2025), reproduced in the 2026 report. They are not findings of the 2,300 GC interviews and date from 2025.

verdicts.claim: The audience for legal information has structurally expanded: 84% of CLOs report to the CEO and 79% almost always attend board meetings.
verdicts.note: Key Findings PDF read directly: 1,049 participants, 20 industries, 43 countries; 'a record 84% of CLOs now reporting directly to the CEO'; '79% of CLOs now "almost always" attending board meetings'; compliance 64%, corporate secretary 62%; 74% proactive strategic counsel; operational efficiency 53%; budget/resource constraints 35%; 36% active GenAI deployment; 47% say CEO wants tech/AI proficiency. Quote exact. Not verified: the 'sponsored by FTI Technology' attribution. The PDF names no sponsor and acc.com HTML pages return 403. The 2026-01 date rests on the file path only; no field dates given.

verdicts.claim: Legal technology is moving from a departmental expense to a shared enterprise resource, especially at large companies.
verdicts.note: Full PDF read: 576 departments, 45 countries, 'survey opened on February 11, 2026, and closed on April 17, 2026'. 53% entirely within legal; shared services 29% 'up from 25% two years prior'; no tech budget 18%. $5B-$20B: 43% from 29% in 2024; $20B+: 45%. Quote exact. Tech is 3% of total spend, US$130K median for all departments, US$2.5M at $20B+. 0.43% is 'a six-year low' (previous high 0.63%); 367 employees per lawyer; 8:1 lawyers per legal ops professional; legal ops 5% since 2022. Text search confirms no BI/analytics/intake questions. 'June 2026' publication rests on the file path. Reuse flag: the report's copyright notice requires 'Reprinted with permission from the Association of Corporate Counsel 2026. All Rights Reserved.' on extracts and prohibits uploading into AI tools.

verdicts.claim: CLOC's 2026 State of the Industry shows technology strategy and financial management as the top legal ops priorities amid a 'structural productivity gap'.
verdicts.note: CLOC release dated March 2, 2026: '135 law departments representing more than 15 industries and organizations with median revenues of $13 billion'; 'The 2026 findings reveal a structural productivity gap'; 80/72/62; 85% dedicated AI oversight/resources; 37% (from 58%); 47% (from 65%); 32% lawyer headcount. Quote exact, speaker Oyango Snell, CLOC President & CEO. Harbor PRWeb release dated December 8, 2025 confirms the same figures (adds headcount 32% down from 42%). Neither release nor the CLOC blog mentions analytics, dashboards, BI or intake. Field dates not published.

verdicts.claim: ACC's own definition of 'Advanced' metrics maturity is self-service dashboards plus predictive analytics; data integrity is the named early-stage hurdle.
verdicts.note: PDF read directly. All three quoted strings are exact ('Uneven integrity/cleanliness of data; working to improve data integrity through naming conventions, standard groupings'; 'Most metrics generated through manual synthesis of data from disparate systems'; the dashboards sentence). Advanced stage also lists leading/lagging indicators, central data source, predictive analytics, and an annual review where metrics are 'pressure-tested'. Minor: table of contents calls the function 'Metrics & Analysis' while the section header reads 'METRICS & ANALYTICS'. Version date remains unknown: the PDF says only that the original model was published in 2017.

verdicts.claim: Gartner predicts AI-driven intake will capture all requests at 60% of legal departments and answer half without human intervention by 2029; legal tech budgets double by 2028.
verdicts.note: Confirmed as reported by trade press only. Lawyers Weekly, Grace Robbie, June 9, 2026: quote exact, speaker Weston Wicks, Senior Director Analyst, Gartner Legal and Compliance Practice; 'By 2029, approximately 50 per cent of contract reviews will be delegated to self-service systems that escalate only one in 10 for human review'; spending 'will double within just three years'. The article does not state the Gartner release date; gartner.com returned 403, so '2026-05-26' rests only on a URL slug and is unverified. Second item confirmed in Lawyers Weekly July 28, 2026 (Grace Robbie): '56 per cent of legal departments anticipate a headcount freeze or reduction in 2026', analyst Raashi Rastogi; the 2026-07-15 Gartner release date is unverified. Cite as Gartner via Lawyers Weekly, and label as forecasts.

verdicts.claim: Vendors are explicitly positioning natural-language answers embedded in workflow as the successor to dashboards.
verdicts.note: Legal.io release read directly (Chicago, May 11, 2026). Attribution the finding omits: 'In-house teams don't need another dashboard. They need answers.' is said by Pieter Gunst, CEO of Legal.io, not the COO. The 'stitching that data together manually' quote is Hannah Konitshek, COO, exact. Mitratech release (Austin, May 11, 2026): ARIES 'tracks spend against budget in real time within the matter view, and answers natural-language questions about outside counsel performance'. Wolters Kluwer release (Houston, May 5, 2026): 'Natural Language controls: Legal teams can interrogate invoices for spend and compliance trends'. All vendor marketing.

verdicts.claim: Legal data is now an input to agents that act, not only to reports: agentic invoice adjustment, conversation-to-matter intake, and AI-maintained matter status.
verdicts.note: All three releases read directly. Wolters Kluwer (May 5, 2026): 'identifies non-compliant invoice line items and automatically implements adjustments'; 'fully auditable and reversible'; 'more than $200 billion in actual legal invoice data'; quote exact, speaker Dean Sonderegger, SVP & GM, Wolters Kluwer ELM Solutions. Checkbox (May 11, 2026): agent can 'automatically create a fully populated matter on the legal board and kick off the right workflow'. Streamline AI (Burlingame, May 11, 2026): 'orchestrate a system of interconnected AI agents'; Kathy Zhu quote exact. Legal IT Insider, Toby Weston, May 15, 2026, 'CLOC Global Institute 2026: a market in transition' confirms embedded intelligence, workflow automation and integration as 'the new battleground'.

verdicts.claim: Cycle time is being reframed as the key intake metric, and its historical weakness is a data-quality problem (humans updating matter status).
verdicts.note: Checkbox release read directly (New York, May 11, 2026). Quote exact. Also exact: 'reliable data has traditionally depended on whether someone remembered to move a matter from "In Review" to "Awaiting Business"'; 'accurately distinguishing time spent by legal from time spent waiting on the business'; 'answered instantly, escalated into a process, or routed to the right attorney'; 'report on SLAs'. The TR LDO cross-reference holds (cycle time under 15% in Figure 3; TR's own article says 'less than 20%'). The framing 'key intake metric' is the vendor's claim, not an independent finding. Streamline's 93.7% benchmark was not checked and should stay out.

verdicts.claim: Measurement of AI value is the new metrics frontier: 83% of in-house teams cannot measure whether AI spend is working and only 7% have scaled AI.
verdicts.note: Axiom page (June 29, 2026): 'Based on a survey of 528 in-house legal leaders across six countries, conducted by InsightDynamo for Axiom in March 2026'; 83% 'cannot measure whether their AI spending is working'; 7% 'have actually scaled AI across the organization'. Vendor (ALSP) research. Supporting items: TR landing-page line confirmed; FTI/Relativity release March 11, 2026 confirmed (224 survey respondents summer 2025, 30 interviews Sept 2025, 87% vs 44%, roadmap 53% vs 25%); RLLB 'The AI ROI Playbook for Legal Teams' confirmed on the event site. Blickstein 23% 'fully operational' and usability-over-security seen only in a secondary Integreon webinar recap (July 9, 2026); Blickstein's own site says 'more than 70 companies', not 68-70.

verdicts.claim: Agentic workflows are reaching production in legal, with stale data already causing incidents; self-assessed readiness far exceeds tested readiness.
verdicts.note: The page does say what the finding reports (June 17, 2026; n=200 = AmLaw 200 n=84, regional firms n=61, Fortune 1000 in-house n=55; 38%/47%/54%; 58% vs 11%; 22% stale-data incidents; 11% of e-billing users). I cannot treat it as credible. The About page names no people, no organisation and no location, publishes without bylines, and states that AI tools are used for research and drafting. The stated 'margin of error ±4.8% at 95% confidence' is arithmetically inconsistent with n=200 (which gives ±6.9%; ±4.8% needs about n=417). No independent corroboration found. Recommend not citing. The ILTA comparison is solid: eDiscovery Today Sept 14, 2026, '508 firms', '13% of respondents said they are already using Agentic AI on the business side or in practice' (law firms, not in-house).

verdicts.claim: CFO-legal budgeting is shifting toward value-based models, with a perception gap over who controls the legal budget.
verdicts.note: Axiom page confirms: released September 8, 2025; 500+ GCs, CLOs, deputy GCs and CFOs; eight countries; '49% of legal departments transformed their budgeting models in the past 12 months, with another 36% planning changes'; '78% are mandated to implement AI without dedicated budgets'; '89% of legal leaders rate CFO relationships as excellent, but a 18-point authority gap undermines strategic collaboration'. Field dates not stated. Vendor research.
verdicts.corrected_detail: The 50% of CFOs vs 32% of legal leaders breakdown behind the '18-point authority gap' does not appear on the public page and was not seen; the arithmetic fits but it rests on a search snippet. The interpretation that the gap concerns 'who controls legal budget-setting' is likewise not stated on the public page. Print only the 18-point figure unless the gated report is obtained.

verdicts.claim: Conference facts: CLOC Global Institute ran May 11-14, 2026 in Chicago and launched the Compass maturity platform; ILTACON 2026 ran Aug 23-27 in Nashville; RLLB 2026 ran Sept 8-11 in Las Vegas.
verdicts.note: CGI: May 11-14, 2026, Chicago, 2,300+ attendees on CLOC's news hub; Legal.io release adds McCormick Place. Compass: CLOC release May 12, 2026, Neota Logic, companion to the Core 12 Maturity Assessment Playbook, four stages, beta, members only; quote exact, speaker Oyango Snell. CLOC does not list the four areas or stage names; those come only from Steno's recap (June 3, 2026), which also reports Mike Haven (Meta) with 'Deflection' as the first of four pillars, defined as 'Legal embedded into business workflows'. RLLB: September 8-11, 2026, Fontainebleau Las Vegas, 900+ attendees, 100+ sessions, confirmed on the event site. ILTACON: Gaylord Opryland, Nashville confirmed by ILTA's wrap-up page (5,780 attendees, 241 booths); the Aug 23-27 dates and '80+ sessions' were seen only on a vendor blog (joinajax.com) because ILTA's pages now show 2027.

verify:bi-analytics-stats.overall_note:
Twelve of the 15 findings are confirmed, two are corrected and one is unverified. I read every primary source URL the researcher gave. The PDFs (TR LDO Index, TR 2026 State of the Corporate Law Department, ACC CLO key findings, ACC/MLA benchmarking, ACC Maturity Model, and five CLOC Global Institute press releases) were downloaded and text-extracted locally, so quotes and numbers were checked against the full text rather than summaries.

The session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200 of 200), so I could not search independently for primary sources. Verification used the given URLs, URLs in the researcher's own notes, and publisher pages. I did not route around the cap through a search engine.

Points the writer should act on:
- **Finding 3 (TR 2026 State report):** two sub-statistics are borrowed from other TR reports. The 19%/39% "decision-making using analytics" figures come from the Future of Professionals Report 2025. The 47% GenAI-access figure comes from the 2026 AI in Professional Services Report.
- **Finding 13 (The Legal Stack):** do not cite it. The publisher is anonymous, publishes without bylines, and says it drafts with AI tools. Its stated margin of error of ±4.8% is impossible for n=200, which gives ±6.9%.
- **Finding 14 (Axiom budgeting):** the 50%/32% breakdown behind the "18-point authority gap" is not on the public page. Print only the 18-point figure.
- **Finding 9 (Legal.io):** the "don't need another dashboard" quote belongs to Pieter Gunst, CEO. The finding left it unattributed.
- **Finding 8 (Gartner):** both items are confirmed only through Lawyers Weekly. The Gartner release dates of 2026-05-26 and 2026-07-15 are unverified because gartner.com returns 403.
- **Finding 4 (ACC CLO Survey):** FTI Technology's sponsorship is unverified, because acc.com HTML pages return 403 and the key-findings PDF names no sponsor.
- **Finding 5 (ACC/MLA benchmarking):** the report's copyright notice requires "Reprinted with permission" wording on extracts and prohibits uploading the report into AI tools.
- **Finding 15 (ILTACON 2026):** the Aug 23-27 dates and "80+ sessions" were seen only on a vendor blog. The Nashville venue is confirmed by ILTA's own wrap-up page.

The verification notes are at C:/Users/RALPHS~1/AppData/Local/Temp/claude/c--code-files-spaarke-website/aa6b682a-4844-485c-99e0-cb2228b928c3/scratchpad/research/bi-analytics-stats.verified.md, and the text extracts of the PDFs are in the fc/ subfolder beside it. No file in any git repository was modified.

verdicts.claim: Wikipedia's 'Signs of AI writing' is the most complete, actively maintained catalog, and it warns that the signs are symptoms, not the problem to fix.
verdicts.note: Read the raw wikitext. Quote is exact and bolded in the lead; preceding sentence says the patterns are 'only potential signs of a problem, not the problem itself'. Caution exact: 'Not all text featuring these indicators is AI-generated...'. Latest revision seen 21 Sep 2026 14:31. WikiProject AI Cleanup first revision 2023-12-04 (Wikipedia API). All named tells exist. Minor: the heading is 'Language and grammar', not 'Language'. The page carries an August 2026 {{update}} banner for recent models, calls itself 'descriptive, not prescriptive', and warns some signs 'may not apply in a non-Wikipedia context'. 'Most complete' is researcher judgement.

verdicts.claim: AI vocabulary tells shift by model generation; 'delve' has largely receded, so word lists age quickly and density matters more than any single word.
verdicts.note: Era table verified word for word in the wikitext: 2023 to mid-2024 (GPT-4), mid-2024 to mid-2025 (GPT-4o), mid-2025 and on (GPT-5: emphasizing, enhance, highlighting, showcasing, plus words from the 'canned emphasis on notability' section). Delve sentence exact: 'became less frequent later in 2024, then dropped off sharply in 2025' (cites Washington Post 2025-11-13 and Geng and Trotta). Quote exact. Extra caution on the page: a word being overused 'does not imply that its synonyms are also overused'.

verdicts.claim: Peer-reviewed word-frequency analysis found at least 13.5% of 2024 PubMed abstracts were processed with LLMs, detected through excess 'style' words.
verdicts.note: Seen in arXiv HTML v5 (2025-07-03), identical to the figures cited: 15.1M abstracts 2010-2024; 13.5% lower bound; 'reaching 40% for some subcorpora' (discussion: 'above 30%'); 454 excess words in 2024 vs 190 in 2021; delves r=28.0, underscores 13.8, showcasing 10.7; potential, findings, crucial by frequency gap. Precision: the 66% verbs / 14% adjectives split applies to the 379 excess style words, not all 454. Journal ref Science Advances 11(27), 2 July 2025, DOI 10.1126/sciadv.adt3813 (Crossref). Authors: Kobak, Gonzalez-Marquez, Horvat, Lause.

verdicts.claim: The present-participle tail and noun-heavy density are measurable: instruction-tuned LLMs use present participial clauses at 2 to 5 times the human rate.
verdicts.note: Seen in arXiv HTML v2: '2 to 5 times the rate of human text'; GPT-4o 5.3x (d=1.38), 'that' clauses as subject 2.6x, nominalizations 2.1x, phrasal coordination 1.9x, agentless passive 'roughly half'; Table 1 camaraderie 162, tapestry 155, intricate 119; 'informationally dense, noun-heavy style'. Two details: the quote is mid-sentence in the paper ('Also, instruction tuning appears to make the model output less human, not more: ...'), so the capital I is not original; and 2025-08-21 is only the arXiv v2 date. PNAS publication date per Crossref is 2025-02-18, vol. 122 issue 8, DOI 10.1073/pnas.2422455122.

verdicts.claim: Frequent LLM users are near-perfect detectors of AI text, and the clues they cite most are vocabulary and sentence structure, followed by punctuation, originality, quotations, over-explanation, formatting and formula conclusions.
verdicts.corrected_detail: Quote is not exact. The paper reads: "The quotes also feel fake, every expert speaks the same way and it's too homogenous with the text." Also, the 'Grammar & Punctuation' category (24.8%) is defined as AI text being 'usually grammatically perfect (also avoiding dashes and ellipses)', so in this study dashes were read as a human marker, which cuts against using it to support the em dash tell.
verdicts.note: All numbers seen in arXiv HTML: 300 articles; majority vote of five experts 'misclassifies only 1 of 300'; nonexperts avg TPR 56.7% (FPR 52.5% in text, 51.7 in table); experts avg TPR 92.7%, FPR 4.0%; clue shares 53.1 / 35.9 / 24.8 / 23.7 / 22.3 / 19.5 / 15.0 / 13.1 all match. Formatting is defined as 'fully capitalized headings, bolded lists, paragraphs of similar length'. Models tested were GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o1-Pro. ACL 2025 long paper pp. 5342-5373, DOI 10.18653/v1/2025.acl-long.267. The closing inference about Spaarke's readers is the researcher's, not the paper's.

verdicts.claim: Em dash frequency is model-specific rather than universal: 0 to 10.6 per 1,000 words across twelve models, against a human essay mean of 3.23 with a 50-fold human range.
verdicts.note: Seen in arXiv HTML Table 1: GPT-4.1 10.62 (9.10 suppressed), Claude Opus 4.6 9.09 (0.19), DeepSeek V3 6.95 (5.41), Gemini 2.5 Pro 3.53 (0.00), both Llama Instruct models 0.00; also GPT-4o 4.12, GPT-5.4 1.43. Human baseline: eight essays, 57,232 words, weighted mean 3.23, median 3.83, range 0.33-17.12. Quote exact. Single author (E. M. Freeburg), 14 pages, no journal reference, no peer review. '50-fold' is the researcher's arithmetic (17.12/0.33 = 52), not the paper's wording, and the human baseline is very small.

verdicts.claim: Wikipedia's em dash tell is about placement as well as frequency: models use em dashes where people would use commas, parentheses or colons, which maps directly onto a replacement guide.
verdicts.corrected_detail: The 'unidentified July 2026 study' is identified in the page's reference: The Economist, 'How to spot AI writing', 30 July 2026 (https://www.economist.com/culture/2026/07/30/how-to-spot-ai-writing). Wikipedia says AI em dashes are 'usually surrounded by spaces' (not 'often'). A September 2026 banner now heads the section saying the sign 'seems to be less common in current LLM output' and may be moved to historical indicators.
verdicts.note: Quote exact in the wikitext; the full sentence compares LLM output with 'nonprofessional human-written text of the same genre'. Wikipedia sentence on the study: 'of contemporary models only Claude used em dashes more than professional writers, and ChatGPT used them less.' I could not open The Economist (403, no Wayback copy), so its underlying numbers are unverified. The section also says the sign 'is most useful when taken in combination with other indicators, not by itself'.

verdicts.claim: OpenAI publicly treated ChatGPT's em dash habit as a defect to fix, confirming the mark's status as a recognized tell.
verdicts.note: TechCrunch, Sarah Perez, 2025-11-14. Full Altman post on X: 'Small-but-happy win: If you tell ChatGPT not to use em-dashes in your custom instructions, it finally does what it's supposed to do!' The cited quote is an exact substring. Article lists 'school papers, emails, comments, customer service chats, LinkedIn posts, online forums, ad copy' and says it 'won't necessarily eliminate the em dash from its output by default'. Corroborated by the Ars Technica piece (Benj Edwards, same date) cited on Wikipedia, which ties it to GPT-5.1.

verdicts.claim: Style authorities agree every em dash function has a more formal substitute: comma pair, parentheses, colon, semicolon or full stop.
verdicts.note: Punctuation Guide quotes seen: 'can take the place of commas, parentheses, or colons'; 'always more emphatic than commas'; 'Dashes are considered less formal than parentheses; they are also more intrusive'; 'The dash is less formal than the colon'; 'best limited to two appearances per sentence'. CMOS Q&A item located (faq0181, 18th ed.): 'You're right that a semicolon or a period might be better than a dash in that example' and 'Because dashes are so flexible, they tend to be overused. When in doubt, edit them out.' The same answer also says a dash 'really can be used in place of just about any mark of punctuation', so 'authorities agree' is a synthesis. Wikipedia 'Dash' confirms Penguin/CUP/Routledge spaced en dash ('not universal'; OUP differs), typewriter double hyphen, en dash for closed ranges.

verdicts.claim: The em dash is weak evidence of authorship even though it is a strong trigger of suspicion; defenders note that canonical human prose matches or exceeds model rates.
verdicts.corrected_detail: The phrase 'much smaller and noisier than the myth suggests' is not on the page; actual wording: 'It's just a lot smaller and a lot noisier than "AI uses em dashes and humans don't."' Also, as fetched today the page never uses the word 'peer'; it labels Freeburg '(arXiv, 2026)', 'a controlled study' and 'the cleanest public measurement we found'. Drop the statement that the vendor calls it peer-reviewed.
verdicts.note: Numbers seen: Huckleberry Finn 10.13, Moby-Dick 8.12, pooled 4.76 em dashes per 1,000 over 702,939 words, GPT-4.1 10.62 (taken from Freeburg). 'A dash is a keystroke, not a thought.' exact; 'weighted deliberately low' on page; dated Jul 31, 2026. The Ringer confirmed: Brian Phillips, 'Stop AI-Shaming Our Precious, Kindly Em Dashes—Please', 2025-08-20, arguing models learned the mark from human books. Comparators are nineteenth-century novels, not business prose; source is a detection vendor.

verdicts.claim: Negative parallelism ('it is not X, it is Y') is reported as the most durable AI tell, about three times more frequent in LLM text than human text, and is spreading into corporate filings.
verdicts.corrected_detail: The threefold figure is a Pangram (AI-detection vendor) estimate quoted by The Atlantic, and it covers 'Not just X but Y' sentences: 'three times as often in AI writing as they do in human writing'. The Atlantic reports Barron's found the construction 'in corporate communications more than quadrupled from 2023 to 2025'; Barron's lede names conference calls, shareholder letters and news releases, not 'Fortune 500 filings', and the raw counts (about 50 to 200+) were not seen (paywall). Washington Post wording is '6 percent of chats in July' (July 2025), not messages. 'Most durable' is the researcher's gloss; The Atlantic says 'perhaps the best-known tic'.
verdicts.note: I retrieved the opening of The Atlantic piece directly (Will Oremus, published 2026-07-12): the Pangram sentence, the Barron's sentence and 'has shown no signs of abating' (contrasted with delve) are verbatim. Pangram primary page: 'AI uses phrases that fit this template three times as often as humans' (https://www.pangram.com/supporting-evidence). Barron's: Shaina Mishkin, 'AI Is Changing How Companies Talk to Shareholders. Here Is the Red Flag for Readers.', 2026-04-14. WaPo (Merrill, Chen, Kumer, 2025-11-13, via Wayback): 328,744 GPT-4o messages from 37,929 conversations, May 2024 to July 2025. The Wikipedia 'Negative parallelism' article is a one-source stub; cite the primaries instead.

verdicts.claim: The cause of overused vocabulary points to human-feedback training rather than architecture or training data, which explains why the tells read as 'trying to sound good'.
verdicts.note: arXiv abstract read in full: 21 focal words; quote exact; COLING 2025; submitted 2024-12-16. The abstract hedges: 'While the model testing is consistent with RLHF playing a role, our experimental results suggest that participants may be reacting differently to "delve" than to other focal words.' Follow-up arXiv 2508.01930 (2025-08-03, BIAS 2025 at ECML PKDD) confirmed: Llama, 'participants systematically prefer text variants that include certain words', 'LHF workers versus LLM users'. Goedecke post confirmed, 2025-10-30, old print books hypothesis. 'Trying to sound good' is the researcher's interpretation.

verdicts.claim: Practitioner catalogs cover the structural tells that lack academic measurement, and they stress that clustering and repetition, not single uses, give prose away.
verdicts.note: tropes.fyi quote is exact but sits at the end of tropes.md (https://tropes.fyi/tropes-md), not on the home page. Every named trope exists in the directory, including tie-back. 'Launched Feb 2026' could not be confirmed: the changelog's oldest entry is 2026-03-14; v2 (49 tropes, 10 behaviours) shipped 2026-08-14. That changelog also notes double-hyphen dashes are now flagged 'since AI-generated text increasingly uses them as a substitute', which matters for any replacement guide. Rough at Sea dictionary confirmed at https://roughatsea.com/notes/the-llm-ism-dictionary, dated Aug 15, 2026; all five named entries and 'statistically well-behaved' seen. Its entry 86 states 'The em dash is not an AI tell.'

verdicts.claim: AI-preferred vocabulary is entering human speech, so vocabulary-based judgments will increasingly misfire on human writers.
verdicts.note: arXiv abstract read: delve, showcase, boast, intricacies, meticulous 'increased abruptly in spontaneous human speech'; '737,083 hours of conversation from 824,634 podcast episodes'; 'A preregistered experiment (N = 496)'. v1 2024-09-03, v4 2026-07-16; still a preprint. Max Planck affiliation is not shown on the abstract page and was not checked further. The 'will increasingly misfire' conclusion is inference, though Wikipedia's Caveats section makes the same point citing this paper.

verdicts.claim: In professional settings, perceived heavy AI assistance lowers perceived sincerity, which is the business cost of sounding like AI.
verdicts.note: HR Dive (Laurel Kalser, 2025-08-21) seen: 1,100 full-time U.S. professionals; 'More than 8 in 10' vs 'Only 40% to 52%'. Primary identified via Crossref: Cardon and Coman, 'Professionalism and Trustworthiness in AI-Assisted Workplace Writing: The Benefits and Drawbacks of Writing With AI', International Journal of Business Communication, online 2025-07-16, vol. 63(4), DOI 10.1177/23294884251350599. Its abstract confirms 1,100 working professionals and that at 'medium- to high-levels of AI assistance' respondents 'question the authorship, confidence, caring, sincerity, and ability of senders'. Percentages appear only in the secondary report. Design caveat: respondents were told the AI-assistance level for a congratulatory team email, so it measures reaction to known AI use, not detection by style.

verify:ai-writing-tells.overall_note:
I checked all 15 findings myself. 11 are confirmed, 4 need corrections (5, 7, 10, 11), and none is refuted. The web search budget was already exhausted, so I located primaries by following citations and by Crossref, OpenAlex and Wayback lookups. All figures taken from papers were checked directly against the papers or Crossref and match.

Corrections to make before publishing:
- **Finding 5 (Russell et al.):** the quote is not exact. The paper reads "The quotes also feel fake, every expert speaks the same way and it's too homogenous with the text." The same paper treats dashes as a human marker (AI text "avoiding dashes and ellipses"), so do not cite it in support of the em dash tell.
- **Finding 7 (Wikipedia em dash section):** the "unidentified July 2026 study" is identified in the page's reference list. It is The Economist, "How to spot AI writing", 30 July 2026. The section now carries a September 2026 banner saying the em dash sign "seems to be less common in current LLM output".
- **Finding 10 (SlopDetector):** the phrase "much smaller and noisier than the myth suggests" is not on the page. The actual wording is "a lot smaller and a lot noisier than 'AI uses em dashes and humans don't.'" The page does not call Freeburg's paper peer-reviewed; it labels it "(arXiv, 2026)". Drop that statement.
- **Finding 11 (negative parallelism):**
  - The threefold figure is a vendor estimate from Pangram, quoted by The Atlantic, and it covers "Not just X but Y" sentences only.
  - The Barron's finding, as The Atlantic reports it, is "corporate communications more than quadrupled from 2023 to 2025". I did not see the raw counts (about 50 to 200+) or the "Fortune 500 filings" framing.
  - The Washington Post figure is "6 percent of chats in July" 2025, not messages.
  - "Most durable" is the research agent's wording, not the source's.

Smaller points:
- **Reinhart:** the PNAS publication date is 2025-02-18; 2025-08-21 is only the arXiv v2 date. The quote is mid-sentence in the paper, so the capital "I" is not original.
- **Kobak:** the 66% verbs and 14% adjectives split applies to the 379 excess style words, not to all 454 excess words.
- **Freeburg:** "50-fold" is the research agent's arithmetic (17.12 / 0.33), not the paper's wording, and the human baseline is only eight essays.

MIT SMR 'When Not to Use AI' (Benjamin Laker, March 30, 2026) ends 'Let the machine do the lifting, not the leading.' Deloitte agents article closer exact (last sentence before Methodology); its printed date is 10 Sep. 2026 rather than 9 Sep. The generalization across all articles is researcher analysis.

verdicts.claim: Eight opening patterns recur; the most reusable for a general counsel audience is 'received view, then reversal' backed by the author's own evidence.
verdicts.note: All eight example openings checked against full text: HBR 2026-09-21 first sentence exact, reversal line at ~word 60; HBR 2026-09-17 (Guido Friebel) opens on named scene 'Linus Arauz operates 10 points of sale...'; HBR Dec 2004 (Larry Downes, 'First, Empower All the Lawyers') opens 'Your company's legal department is broken.'; HBR Jul 2012 (Ertel and Gordon) 'That close relationship is being disrupted.' at ~word 95; HBR 2016-07-25 (Heineman) 'What receives far less attention...'; Deloitte knowledge article opens with US$6.9-9.6 trillion then 'In boardrooms across America, a question is surfacing...' (printed date 18 June 2026, not 17 June); Deloitte C-suite opens with the plain question (printed 18 Dec. 2025). 'Most reusable' is a recommendation, not a fact.

verdicts.claim: Measured rhythm: average sentence length of about 15 to 25 words in 14 of 16 articles, 10 to 25 percent of HBR sentences at eight words or fewer, and paragraphs averaging 50 to 80 words; practice is less austere than writing-coach advice.
verdicts.note: Quote exact. I recomputed with regex on eight HBR article bodies: averages 15.2, 15.6, 16.6, 16.9, 18.0, 19.0, 24.9 and 27.8 (Heineman 2016 is the outlier; finding says 'about 30'); share of sentences <= 8 words 10% to 26%; every article had sentences of 30+ words (2 to 51). Bain 2019 body paragraphs average 76.9 words (matches 77); MIT SMR column ~54-57. Deloitte and s+b paragraph means and the full 16-article tally not recomputed. Attribution note: Garner is quoted in the 2014 HBR guide; Bernoff's advice is in his own HBR article (2016-09-06), not the 2014 piece.

verdicts.claim: Legal-trained writers must invert their habitual structure, and practitioners explicitly treat McKinsey Quarterly as a style model.
verdicts.note: Carolyn O'Hara, HBR, 2014-11-20; full text read via JSON-LD. David McCombie (Harvard Law School to McKinsey) told to 'get to the point more quickly'; quote exact: 'But in business communications, it's best to start with your conclusion first.' Tim Glowa, 'a strategic marketing consultant', 'began reading business publications, like McKinsey Quarterly, for style' (exact). Garner 'great diseases' quote exact; contractions, -ion words to action verbs, and the buzzword blacklist (actionable, core competency, impactful, incentivize) confirmed. Caveat: the 'practitioners treat McKinsey Quarterly as a style model' generalization rests on this single case study, and Glowa is a marketing consultant, not a McKinsey consultant.

completeness-critic.assessment:
The sweep is strong on Article 3 (platform model), on the context-layer landscape for Article 4, on how the industry frames KM for Article 5, and on the voice update's AI-tells catalog and local audit. Articles 1 and 2 have the largest gaps.

I worked from the digest and a keyword search of the notes in C:\code_files\spaarke-website\content-platform\research\2026-09-loi-series\notes\. I ran no web searches.

**1. Association definitions are missing for Article 1.**
- Article 1 must open on CLOC, ACC and "Legal Operators" definitions of legal operations.
- The notes hold only a "closest thing found" definition for LegalOps.com, read from its staging mirror.
- They hold nothing on CLOC's own definition or its Core 12 (the twelve core competencies) list.
- They hold no ACC definition; the ACC Maturity Model 2.0 appears only in its Metrics and KM slices.
- They hold no framing from legaloperators.com, which the research showed is a different organization from the one the brief named.
- The Article 1 writer has to decide which organization the brief meant and needs verbatim text from each. The KM finding (both frameworks define KM without mentioning AI) and the BI finding (how each frames metrics) depend on the same primary documents.

**2. Article 2's core thesis was not researched.**
- The BI track gathered legal-department statistics only.
- A keyword search of bi-analytics-stats.md finds no hits for Power BI, semantic layer, Tableau, ThoughtSpot or deterministic. Evidence may exist under other wording, because I did not read the file in full.
- No evidence was found for "BI is becoming more sophisticated, easy to use, on demand", "BI as the deterministic dimension" or "BI outputs as inputs to agents".
- The ontology track touched Power BI semantic models only as a Fabric IQ input.

**3. Intake and self-service evidence is mostly vendor marketing.**
- Two tracks flagged this gap.
- Evidence found so far:
  - One Gartner forecast, read only through secondary reprints.
  - Juro's vendor survey (13% already running routine contracts without daily legal involvement).
  - Undisclosed-methodology vendor claims from Streamline AI and Checkbox.
- Articles 1 and 2 both need a worked intake example with real numbers.

**4. Article 4's demand-side claims lack corporate-legal evidence.**
- The claims are that departments want control, want to build their own solutions, and need open vendors.
- The three searches that would have tested them never ran.
- The only build-versus-buy survey data found is law-firm data.
- The list of enterprise legal management (ELM) and contract lifecycle management (CLM) vendors with "no MCP announcement" rests on searches, not on reading vendor sites: Mitratech, Onit, LawVu, Checkbox, Icertis and Agiloft. That is a risk if the article names or implies closed vendors.
- No statistic exists on system fragmentation in legal departments, which both Article 3's "consolidates information from all sources" premise and Article 4 need.

**5. Conference coverage is thin.**
- The brief explicitly asks for it (CLOC, RLLB, ACC, ILTACON).
- ILTACON 2026 KM and data sessions were never searched.
- No session-level content was retrieved for CLOC Global Institute (CGI) 2026.
- RLLB has one vendor recap; trade-press recaps may have appeared since.

**6. The voice guide has no verbatim McKinsey text.**
- The user named McKinsey first.
- The McKinsey conventions in the notes come from prior knowledge, not verified sources.

**Not worth a task.**
- The "legal is second after coding" investment statistic has no source. Drop it from the articles unless someone finds one; a plausible lead is the Menlo Ventures 2025 enterprise generative AI report on vertical AI spend, which I did not check.
- Re-checking quotes read through the summarizing fetch tool is a pre-publication editing step, not research. The exception is the Gartner intake prediction, folded into task 3 because two articles use it.
- Byline and contact-line choices are the user's decisions.

gap:intake-and-self-service-named-cases.summary:
WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) when this task began, so zero searches ran; all evidence comes from about 60 direct WebFetch calls. gartner.com, acc.com, legalops.com and web.archive.org were blocked, and CLOC agenda pages render client-side. ACC Value Champions, CLOC/LegalOps.com awards, CCBJ and WorldCC benchmarks were therefore NOT reached and remain gaps.

Gartner: two independent reprints (SMBtech 2026-05-27, carrying release boilerplate; Lawyers Weekly 2026-06-09) match word for word. It is a direct quote from analyst Weston Wicks, release dated 2026-05-26, horizon 2029, population simply "legal departments" with no survey or sample. Correct wording is "without human intervention", and "one-half" refers to requests captured by adopting departments.

Best non-vendor named cases come from ACC Corporate Counsel Now (2026-09-16): Liberty Mutual reviews about 2,500 NDAs a year, lawyer handling cut from over an hour to 15-20 minutes, self-service tool still in pilot; Palo Alto Networks cut routine turnaround from three-to-five days to one, saving 20-40 hours monthly, and is the only case listing intake fields. ACC/Everlaw 2026: only 28 percent of teams track time to resolution.

Vendor-published named cases (Checkbox, Streamline AI, Josef, Juro) give NDA-specific deflection (Coca-Cola Europacific Partners 90 percent; Align 5-7 percent needing redlines) and cycle time (Elastic 23 to 3 days). No case publishes a whole-front-door deflection rate. Tool results also carried a repeated injected reminder block, which I ignored and flagged.

findings.claim: Gartner's 2029 intake prediction is a direct analyst quote from a press release dated 2026-05-26, with population stated only as 'legal departments' and no survey basis; correct wording is 'without human intervention'.
findings.detail: Primary gartner.com release returned 403. Verified against two independent reprints that match word for word. SMBtech carries release boilerplate (report name 'Innovation Insight: Legal AI Platforms', conference plug), marking it as a near-verbatim syndication. Speaker: Weston Wicks, Senior Director Analyst, Gartner Legal & Compliance Practice. The 2029 horizon is inherited from the prior sentence ('In the same timeframe'). 'One-half' refers to requests captured by the adopting 60% of departments. AU spelling 'per cent' is the reprint's; US original likely '60%'.
findings.exact_quote: we predict that 60 per cent of legal departments will use AI-driven intake systems that capture all requests and answer one-half of those without human intervention
findings.source_title: Gartner Predicts Legal Tech Budgets To Double By 2028 As AI Use Expands Across Legal Departments

findings.claim: Lawyers Weekly independently reproduces the same Gartner intake sentence as a direct quote from Weston Wicks, with no methodology or population given.
findings.detail: Second reprint, by Grace Robbie. Wording identical apart from 'time frame' vs 'timeframe'. Companion prediction: about 50 per cent of contract reviews delegated to self-service systems escalating one in 10 by 2029. Secondary source only; primary release at gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-05-26-gartner-predicts-legal-tech-budgets-to-double-by-2028-as-legal-ai-use-expands not fetchable.
findings.exact_quote: By 2029, approximately 50 per cent of contract reviews will be delegated to self-service systems that escalate only one in 10 for human review.
findings.source_title: Legal tech spending set to double by 2028 amid AI boom

findings.claim: Liberty Mutual's Enterprise Legal Solutions reviews about 2,500 NDAs a year; earlier improvements cut lawyer handling from over an hour to 15-20 minutes per NDA; a self-service AI NDA review tool is now in pilot.
findings.detail: Named person: Nora Marantz, VP and Assistant General Counsel. Tool built by Liberty's internal Legal Data Science team. Underwriters submit NDAs and get immediate AI feedback against US-specific requirements; attorney review reserved for complex agreements. Baseline business wait time 24-48 hours. PILOT status: no post-pilot deflection rate. Intake data is the NDA itself; reporting or routing use not described. Member-submitted to ACC, not award-vetted, but non-vendor.
findings.exact_quote: Prior improvements cut lawyer handling time from more than an hour per NDA to 15 to 20 minutes.
findings.source_title: 5 Ways In-house Legal Departments Are Using AI
findings.publisher: ACC Corporate Counsel Now (Association of Corporate Counsel)

findings.claim: Palo Alto Networks' self-service drafting tool cut routine document turnaround from three-to-five business days to one and saves a three-person legal team an estimated 20-40 hours per month.
findings.detail: Named person: Hayden Creque, Director and Senior Corporate Counsel. Built on Google Gemini with pre-approved templates and playbooks. Only case found that states intake fields: counterparty name, contract date, termination date, reason. Output is used by the business directly or sent for expedited legal review. No reporting on intake data described. Self-reported estimate.
findings.exact_quote: Turnaround on routine documents dropped from three-to-five business days to one.
findings.source_title: 5 Ways In-house Legal Departments Are Using AI
findings.publisher: ACC Corporate Counsel Now (Association of Corporate Counsel)

findings.claim: Only 28 percent of legal teams track time to resolution, versus 83 percent tracking outside counsel spend (ACC and Everlaw 2026 survey).
findings.detail: Reported by Blake E. Garcia PhD and Mauro Whiteman of ACC, citing 'The Role of Generative AI in Proving Corporate Law Department Value' (ACC with Everlaw, 2026). Also: 12 percent track outside counsel performance, 9 percent track impact on business outcomes; barriers are lack of time or resources 57 percent, data scattered across systems 50 percent, limited automation tools 43 percent. Sample size not given in the article. Supports the point that intake-derived service metrics are rarely measured.
findings.exact_quote: Outside counsel spend is tracked by 83 percent of teams, but only 28 percent track time to resolution
findings.source_title: Is Your Legal Team's Data Infrastructure AI-Ready?
findings.publisher: ACC Corporate Counsel Now (Association of Corporate Counsel)

findings.claim: Mercado Libre has run a self-service agreement generator ('Legal Kiosk') since 2015 and now has a 20+ person legal operations team, but publishes no deflection numbers.

AI agents now being applied to high-volume dispute responses in Brazil and Chile. Useful as a named precedent that business self-service predates generative AI; no quantified intake metrics.

findings.source_title: 3 Moves Ahead: How Mercado Libre's Jacobo Cohen Imach Is Reimagining the Legal Department
findings.publisher: ACC Corporate Counsel Now (Association of Corporate Counsel)

findings.claim: Coca-Cola Europacific Partners reports 90% of NDAs are created by business users without legal intervention, with the remaining 10% completed in hours.

Page datePublished 2026-07-26 looks like a site rebuild date; the index still labels the customer Coca-Cola Amatil (name retired 2021), so the program is older.

findings.source_title: Coca-Cola Europacific Partners customer story

Letter of Authorization process went from two days to two minutes using compliance data pulled from Salesforce. Self-service workflow shifted the mix toward first-party paper. Best cycle-time decomposition found: the delay sat in pre-legal intake, not in legal review. No share-resolved-without-lawyer figure.
findings.exact_quote: It sometimes took up to 20 days just deciding whose paper we'd use.
findings.source_title: Elastic customer story

Page says 400 NDAs drafted within months and turnaround reduced from weeks to days. The 96% figure has no stated baseline or period. findings.exact_quote: Only 5–7% of NDAs required redlining outside the system
findings.source_title: Align Technology customer story
