gaps: WebSearch was unavailable for the whole task (session budget of 200 searches already exhausted; DuckDuckGo, Bing, Brave and Google via WebFetch were blocked). The instruction to run at least 8 distinct searches could not be met. Coverage relies on direct retrieval of about 75 primary pages plus on-site searches, so relevant sources that I could not guess a URL for may have been missed.

No Gartner text was read directly: gartner.com (newsroom, reprints, Peer Insights) returned HTTP 403. The 2026 Magic Quadrant's market definition, strategic planning assumptions and any Gartner wording on semantic layers, agents or determinism are unverified. Only the citation line (29 June 2026; Ganeshan, Long, Macari) and vendor self-descriptions were confirmed.

Microsoft's and Salesforce/Tableau's positions in the 2026 Magic Quadrant were not verified; powerbi.microsoft.com and tableau.com returned 403. Leaders confirmed from their own pages: Google, ThoughtSpot, Qlik.

No analyst (Gartner, Forrester or BARC) was found using the word 'deterministic' for the BI or metrics layer. That framing is vendor language (dbt Labs, Google Looker, ThoughtSpot, and implicitly Tableau Pulse). Forrester says 'governed context', 'consistency' and 'enterprise infrastructure'.

No independent, peer-reviewed 2025 to 2026 benchmark of semantic-layer versus text-to-SQL accuracy was found. The dbt Labs 2026 rerun is vendor-run (though open source); Google's 'two thirds' figure is internal and unpublished; the data.world and Snowflake studies predate 2025.

The gated BARC Data, BI and Analytics Trend Monitor 2026 full report and the two Forrester reports ('Make Data AI Ready Via Semantic Layer Platforms', 'Combine Semantics, Ontology, And Knowledge Graphs For AI-Ready Data') were not read; only public summaries.

No licensing or seat-count evidence of audience widening beyond vendor self-reported user counts. No independent BI adoption-rate figure for 2025 to 2026 was found (Forrester's 20% figure is from July 2024). The Gartner '80% of business consumers' prediction is second-hand via ThoughtSpot and unverified.

Power BI Copilot monthly feature-summary posts and any Microsoft post on the 2026 Magic Quadrant could not be reached, so the exact GA date of the in-report Copilot pane and any 2026 Power BI user count beyond the March 2026 '35 million' figure are not documented.

Snowflake Intelligence appears in current docs as 'Snowflake CoWork'; no dated rename announcement was found. Genie One GA status is unconfirmed. Exact GA date of Looker Conversational Analytics ('last year', i.e. 2025) not pinned to a day.
Tableau Pulse to Slack and Salesforce Flow automation specifics, and Tableau Next documentation in the Salesforce Help Center, were not retrieved (JavaScript-rendered).
Nothing here is specific to legal departments; this track is BI technology only, by design.
viewpoints: Vendor consensus: every major platform now routes natural-language questions through a governed semantic model (Power BI semantic model, Tableau Semantics, LookML, Snowflake semantic views, Unity Catalog metric views, dbt MetricFlow, ThoughtSpot search tokens), and all pitch that layer as what keeps AI agents trustworthy.

Strict 'call, do not recompute' architectures (dbt MetricFlow, Looker, ThoughtSpot, Tableau Pulse) versus looser 'LLM writes the query, guided by semantics' designs (Power BI Copilot can author new DAX; Genie and Cortex generate SQL). The article should not claim the strict pattern is universal.

Sceptical reading of the accuracy case: dbt's own 2026 rerun shows raw text-to-SQL at 84 to 90% on well-modeled data, up from about 33% in 2023. The durable argument is failure mode and auditability (an error versus a plausible wrong number), not a permanent accuracy gap.

Forrester's position: BI is not dead and gen AI is not replacing it; the semantic layer is becoming enterprise infrastructure and the starting point on a path toward ontologies, knowledge graphs and 'context layers'. This supports Article 4's pairing of BI with an ontology.

BARC's practitioner view is a counterweight to vendor enthusiasm: data quality, security, culture and governance outrank gen AI; only best-in-class organisations prioritise decision automation and embedded analytics.

Maturity caveat: the semantic model and dashboards are mature, but much of the conversational and agentic layer is still preview (Power BI standalone Copilot, Fabric ontology, Looker Agentic Workflows and Dashboard Agents, Genie in Teams and Slack), and the interchange standard (Apache Ossie) is a 0.2.0 draft in incubation.

Product names are churning fast (Genie Spaces to Genie Agents, Snowflake Intelligence shown as CoWork, Cortex Analyst folding into Cortex Agents, Data Cloud to Data 360), so the article should date every product reference.

gap:inhouse-demand-for-openness-and-buil.summary: WebSearch was unavailable (session budget 200/200 spent) and general search engines blocked fetches, so discovery relied on on-site searches (Artificial Lawyer, LawNext, Above the Law, CLOC, vendor sites) and 60+ direct page fetches. Vendor check (c) is largely complete and corrects the earlier list: LawVu announced an MCP server (June 2026) with stated write actions for Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot; Icertis advertises "Agent Interoperability" with Claude, OpenAI, Copilot and Joule plus licensed public APIs. Mitratech, Onit/SimpleLegal, Agiloft, Checkbox, TR Legal Tracker and WK ELM all advertise APIs or extensibility but show no public MCP or third-party agent connector; their AI is embedded (ARIES, Unity agents, Ask AI, TyMetrix agent). None can fairly be called "closed". Survey data (a): no 2025-2026 corporate-legal survey found that measures integration/API as a selection criterion, build-versus-buy, systems per department, or manual reconciliation. Available proxies are mostly vendor-commissioned: Icertis (23% of legal AI tools run in full isolation), Counselwell/Spellbook (36% cite system integration as AI barrier), LegalOn (only ~11% reach connected maturity), Axiom, plus the CLOC chair's "tool overload" remark. ACC/MLA 2026 benchmarking has budget data only. Named corporate builders (b): none verified outside the AI industry. Strongest new non-vendor demand voice: Ken Callander (ex-Uber Head of Legal Ops), Above the Law, June 2026, arguing buyers should pick tools with open, agent-ready, write-capable APIs, while conceding most buyers still use an old RFP rubric.

findings.claim: LawVu has announced an MCP server that lets Claude, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot read AND write to its legal workspace; it should not be on a 'silent on MCP' list.
findings.detail: LawVu article announcing the 'LawVu MCP server'. Initial release lists read actions (search/query matters and contracts, summarize, retrieve knowledge) and write actions: 'Create matters or trigger contract workflows directly from an AI tool' and 'Update matter status, create tasks, and set deadlines from connected AI workflows'. Permissions respect record access per user; audit layer. Page shows June 8, 2026; JSON-LD datePublished is 2026-06-02. Wording is future tense ('will enable'), so GA status is not confirmed. Developer portal developer.lawvu.com exists but docs require registration.
findings.source_title: Connecting AI tools to the legal operating system: Introducing the LawVu MCP Server
findings.exact_quote: Create matters or trigger contract workflows directly from an AI tool

findings.claim: A former Uber Head of Legal Operations argues, in a non-sponsored two-part series, that legal ops buyers should select tools with open, agent-ready, write-capable APIs so departments can build their own agents.
findings.detail: Ken Callander, Managing Principal of Value Strategies LLC, former Head of Legal Operations at Uber. Part 1 (2026-06-15) gives a buildability test: documented API over the full data model, real-time events, structured write-back, service-account auth, agent-scale rate limits, stable data model. Also: 'Those that do not will become closed appliances running someone else's product strategy.' Part 2 (2026-06-23): 'Vendors supply the system of record. The Legal Operations function holds the design.' Important caveat in his own words: 'Most Legal Ops buyers are still scoring vendors against the same RFP rubric they used five years ago', which undercuts any claim that openness is already a mainstream criterion. He is a consultant, not a sitting practitioner. Text verified verbatim from raw HTML.
findings.source_title: Why You Should Choose Legal Ops Tools You Can Build On (Part 1)
findings.exact_quote: Ask the vendor whether you can build an agent that reads from their system, makes a decision, and writes back, all without a user clicking anything.

SECONDARY source only; figures come from the fetch tool's reading of the LawNext article and the primary report was not opened. No 2026 edition located.
findings.source_title: Legal Departments Show Growing AI Adoption But Implementation Challenges Remain, New Survey Finds

findings.claim: LegalOn's 2026 In-House Legal Pulse reports 92% of in-house teams use AI but only about 11% have reached 'connected' or 'full workflow' maturity.
findings.detail: LegalOn landing page gives the 92% / 11% headline and a 64% want vs 15% have gap for post-signature AI; sample size and field dates are not disclosed on the public page. Artificial Lawyer (Aug 18, 2026) reports the breakdown: 54.9% experimentation, 26.5% standardized prompts and workflows, 8.8% connected knowledge, 2% full workflow support. Vendor survey; treat as directional evidence of fragmentation.
findings.source_title: 2026 In-House Legal Pulse
findings.exact_quote: 92% of in-house teams use AI today, but only 11% of teams have reached 'connected' or 'full workflow' maturity

findings.claim: Axiom's 2026 In-House Legal AI Report (528 in-house leaders, six countries) finds 83% cannot measure whether AI spending works and only 7% have scaled AI; it says most teams run AI in tools not built for legal work.
findings.detail: Published June 29, 2026; fielded March 2026 by InsightDynamo. Public page gives four headline statistics (100% plan to raise AI budget; 83% cannot measure; 7% scaled; 98% say outside guidance would help) and the phrase 'why most teams are running AI in tools that were never built for legal work' without a percentage. Full report is gated. Note the URL slug says 2025 but the page is the 2026 edition. Axiom is an ALSP with a commercial interest.
findings.source_title: The 2026 Axiom In-House Legal AI Report
findings.exact_quote: why most teams are running AI in tools that were never built for legal work

findings.claim: The ACC/MLA 2026 Law Department Management Benchmarking report's technology section covers budget only; it has no data on integration, APIs, number of systems or build versus buy.
findings.detail: Checked the locally extracted PDF text. Technology findings: median legal technology spend grows from US$65,000 in the smallest companies to US$2.5 million in the largest; technology share of total spend is highest (5%) under US$1B revenue; 53% of departments hold legal technology spending entirely in their own budget; among companies under US$1B, 61% fully contain it, up from 55% in 2024; larger companies trend toward shared, cross-functional funding. Useful for a 'who controls the tech budget' point, not for openness.
findings.source_title: 2026 ACC/MLA Law Department Management Benchmarking Report (local PDF extract: scratchpad/research/pdf/acc-bench-2026.txt)
findings.publisher: Association of Corporate Counsel / Major, Lindsey & Africa

findings.claim: CLOC's public 2026 State of the Industry material gives no integration or tool-count metric, but CLOC's board chair (Delta Air Lines) names 'tool overload' as a current management concern.
findings.detail: CLOC release Mar 2, 2026: technology strategy 80%, financial management 72%, outside counsel and vendor management 62% (135 departments via Harbor 2025 survey). CLOC blog May 6, 2026 signed by Laura Dieudonne, CLOC Board Chair and Legal Operations and Administration Director, Delta Air Lines. Qualitative only.
findings.source_title: What the Numbers Are Telling Us, and What We Owe Each Other
findings.exact_quote: Departments are applying AI to workflows, research, and productivity, with serious attention to governing adoption and managing tool overload.

findings.claim: CLOC programming in 2026 treats in-house agent building as a live peer activity: a Bay Area roundtable for members who 'have already built your own agents' and a practitioner-led AI Intensive covering workflow and agent design.
findings.detail: CLOC San Francisco virtual roundtable 'Working with Agents (Agentic AI)', page published 2026-02-03, moderated by Deborah Haile, Associate Director, Legal Operations, Gilead Sciences. CLOC AI Intensive press release 2026-08-19: workshops of about 40, first event Oct 27, 2026 in New York, exercises include 'workflow and agent design'; quotes Oyango Snell (CLOC CEO) and Alex Gao (Hilton Worldwide). Indicates demand and activity but names no specific department builds.
findings.source_title: CLOC San Francisco Roundtable: Working with Agents (Agentic AI)
findings.exact_quote: So whether you have already built your own agents, or are just getting started, bring your experiences and questions so we can learn from each other.

findings.claim: No named corporate legal department outside the AI industry could be verified as having built its own tools or agents in 2025-2026; available named examples are law firms, vendors, or statements of use or intent.
findings.detail: Site searches of Artificial Lawyer, LawNext, Above the Law, Legal Dive and ACC Corporate Counsel Now returned only law-firm builders (Clifford Chance, Quinn Emanuel, Freshfields, Kirkland, Willkie) and vendors. Weak in-house signals: Accenture legal (Mindy Lok, Legal CTO) quoted on Anthropic's May 12, 2026 page as having 'put Claude to work on everyday legal matters' (use, not build); HUMAN's Patty Corey forecast (Bloomberg Law, Jan 5, 2026); Parker Poe/BARBRI-Lega workshop on Sept 10, 2026 where in-house counsel including Zach Porfiris, GC of Symphonic Distribution, built AI assistants on a vendor platform (press release). Law.com Corporate Counsel and Bloomberg Law could not be searched.
findings.source_title: Parker Poe Clients & Attorneys Build AI Assistants Together to Help Deliver Better Outcomes

findings.claim: The iManage '32% cite integration complexity' figure is drawn from a cross-industry sample of 3,000+ decision makers, not from corporate legal departments specifically.
findings.detail: iManage Knowledge Work Benchmark Report 2026 landing page: 'over 3000 business and technical decision makers' surveyed globally 'across industries'. No law-firm versus corporate-legal cut is shown on the public page. Other figures: 85% at some stage of AI adoption; 25% say end users use public AI with little oversight; 72% plan DMS upgrades. Do not present the 32% as an in-house legal statistic.
findings.source_title: iManage Knowledge Work Benchmark Report 2026
findings.exact_quote: Yet 32% cite integration complexity as one of the biggest barriers to AI adoption.

findings.claim: ACC/Everlaw 2025 survey of 657 in-house respondents supports the 'more control' claim: 64% expect reduced reliance on law firms as GenAI use in US in-house teams rose to 52% from 23%.
findings.detail: 'Generative AI's Growing Strategic Value for Corporate Law Departments', Everlaw and ACC, published Oct 14, 2025; respondents from US, Europe, Australia and Asia. Also: 60% lack visibility into law firm GenAI use; 61% ready to demand new pricing models; company-wide GenAI bans dropped from 30% to 9%. Speaks to insourcing and control, not to platform openness or building. Read from Everlaw's blog summary; full report gated.
findings.source_title: In-House Teams Turn to GenAI for Efficiency, Raising New Expectations for Law Firms

gaps: WebSearch could not run at all on this track: the session budget was already at 200 of 200, and DuckDuckGo, Brave, Mojeek and Bing blocked or degraded fetch-based searching. The required 8 distinct web searches were replaced by about 25 on-site search pages. Re-run with a raised CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION if this track matters.

No 2025-2026 corporate-legal-department survey was found that measures integration, interoperability or API availability as a technology SELECTION criterion. The only barrier-type figures are Counselwell/Spellbook 36% (mostly Canadian, 2025, secondary source) and Icertis 23% isolation (vendor).
No build-versus-buy or 'built our own' percentage for corporate legal departments was found. The only build-vs-buy data remains law-firm data (Bloomberg Law, June 25, 2026).

No figure for the number of systems or tools in a legal department tech stack, and no figure for the share manually reconciling or reporting disconnected data, was found in any 2025-2026 source reached.
Wolters Kluwer Future Ready Lawyer 2026: wolterskluwer.com returned 403 to every report and newsroom URL; report not checked. Existence of a 2026 edition not confirmed.

EY, Deloitte and KPMG general counsel studies, the FTI/Relativity General Counsel Report 2026, Gartner legal technology releases and Bloomberg Law's legal ops and tech surveys were all unreachable (404 on guessed URLs, 403 or bot walls). Not checked.

Named corporate legal departments outside the AI industry that built their own tools or agents: none verified. Law.com Corporate Counsel (registration wall, no usable search), Bloomberg Law and Legal IT Insider could not be searched; CLOC Global Institute 2026 session abstracts were not located.
Wolters Kluwer ELM vendor check is incomplete: only the Passport product page and a Law.com lede were readable. WK ELM newsroom and LegalVIEW/TyMetrix pages not checked for MCP.

Thomson Reuters developer portal catalog is login-gated, so whether a general Legal Tracker REST API is publicly documented could not be confirmed beyond the AP and data APIs named on the features page.

Icertis 'Agent Interoperability' protocol and write scope are not stated publicly; whether it is MCP-based is unknown. LawVu MCP general availability is not confirmed (announcement uses future tense).
Celonis 2026 Process Optimization Report figures (85% / 76%) cited by Callander via VentureBeat were not checked at source and are cross-industry.
Counselwell/Spellbook and Litera figures come from LawNext summaries; the primary reports were not opened.
viewpoints: Practitioner-consultant (Ken Callander, ex-Uber legal ops): buy systems of record with open, write-capable, agent-ready APIs; keep workflow logic and business rules in-house; vendors that own the workflow logic become a ceiling.

Embedded-AI vendors (Mitratech, Onit, Agiloft, Checkbox, WK): legal teams want AI already inside the system of record, not another tool or a DIY build; Checkbox argues token metering makes self-built tools more expensive over three years.

Open-connector vendors (LawVu, Brightflag, iManage, Docusign, Icertis in part): let the customer's AI tool of choice act on governed legal data, with permissions and audit inherited from the platform.

Survey evidence is thinner than the rhetoric: in-house data shows desire for control over spend and law-firm reliance (ACC/Everlaw) and low integration maturity (LegalOn, Icertis), but no survey shows openness as a buying criterion, and Callander himself says most buyers still use a five-year-old RFP rubric.
Peer-community view (CLOC): agent building is treated as a normal member activity and a training need, alongside concern about governance and tool overload, but without published case studies.
Skeptical trade-press view (Artificial Lawyer, Tromans): adding a frontier model beside a retained stack can duplicate cost; in-house teams adopt AI widely but do little that is connected.

gap:mckinsey-primary-text-for-voice.summary:
ACCESS ROUTE DEVIATED FROM THE BRIEF; read this first. No browser tool existed in this session, WebFetch to mckinsey.com timed out, and one undisguised headless-Chrome request was refused by McKinsey's server, so I stopped there. The text was instead downloaded with curl from Internet Archive snapshots (raw id_ HTML) and parsed locally. WebFetch itself refuses web.archive.org, so this was a workaround, not the requested method. All 54 quotations were script-matched to the parsed text; a human should spot-check a few on the live pages. WebSearch was exhausted; discovery used nine Wayback CDX queries.

Corpus: eight McKinsey Insights/Quarterly articles, 2024-09 to 2026-08, 24,773 words, plus a 2026 Blackstone legal case study, a 2021 legal-department article, and a podcast transcript (excluded).

Results: "percent" is spelled out 138 times against zero "%". Exhibits are cited "(Exhibit 1)" at sentence end, "(exhibit)" when single; exhibit titles are full-sentence findings. Em dashes are routine (median 4.7 per 1,000, closed), so there is no McKinsey/HBR conflict; parentheses (7.8 per 1,000), colon plus capital, and semicolons do the same jobs. Headings are always sentence case but message-bearing only in survey and lessons pieces. Thesis sits in paragraph one. Sentences average 23 words, longer and flatter than HBR. "We" appears throughout; "you" is nearly absent. Statistics attribution differs most: third-party sources often sit only in footnotes.

findings.claim: McKinsey spells out 'percent' in running text: 138 instances of the word against zero '%' signs across eight core articles (24,773 words, 2024-09 to 2026-08). Numbers that start a sentence are spelled out, one through ten are words, ranges use 'to'.
findings.detail: Verifies the prior-knowledge claim in the voice notes. Exceptions: one '30%+' in the 2026 Blackstone client case study and a '%' inside a cited database title in a footnote. HBR, Deloitte, Bain, BCG and s+b all use numerals plus %, so this is a real conflict needing one house rule. Text read from Wayback snapshot 20260827200648, not the live page.
findings.source_title: The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI
findings.exact_quote: Forty percent of respondents from large organizations (those with annual revenues of more than $1 billion) report scaling AI agents, up from 27 percent last year.

findings.claim: McKinsey uses em dashes routinely: 1.4 to 12.7 per 1,000 words per article, median 4.7, pooled 7.1 (5.0 excluding the long report), always closed with no spaces. This matches the HBR range, so there is no McKinsey versus HBR conflict on em dashes.
findings.detail: 177 em dashes in 24,773 words. Highest densities are the most exhortatory pieces (Seizing the agentic AI advantage 12.7; Blackstone case study 15.9). Lowest: Gen AI in corporate functions 1.4; 2021 legal article 0.6. 43 sentences use paired dashes for asides; 90 use a single trailing dash for gloss, reversal, or elaboration. Read from Wayback snapshot 20260422144441.
findings.source_title: One year of agentic AI: Six lessons from the people doing the work
findings.exact_quote: In some cases, they are even retrenching—rehiring people where agents have failed.

findings.claim: The punctuation McKinsey itself uses for em dash jobs: parentheses (7.8 per 1,000 words, more frequent than the dash), colon followed by a capitalized full sentence (4.4 per 1,000), and semicolons (1.7 per 1,000), including a semicolon in a heading for a reversal.
findings.detail: Colon plus capital when a full sentence follows (71 instances); lower case only before fragments and lists (34 instances). Heading example of semicolon reversal: 'It’s not about the agent; it’s about the workflow'. Parentheses carry definitions, 'that is' and 'such as' glosses, exact figures behind rounded ones, and exhibit references.
findings.source_title: One year of agentic AI: Six lessons from the people doing the work
findings.exact_quote: A year into the agentic AI revolution, one lesson is clear: It takes hard work to do it well.

findings.claim: Exhibit reference convention: '(Exhibit 1)' in parentheses, capital E, at the end of the sentence that states the finding; '(exhibit)' lower case and unnumbered when there is only one. Exhibit titles are full-sentence, message-bearing findings.
findings.detail: All 17 exhibits in the 2026 State of AI article are cited this way in order. Single-exhibit form from the COO article: 'Multiagent systems can achieve even more (exhibit).' Exhibit title read from alt text in the 2025 edition: 'Larger companies lead the way in scaling AI beyond pilots.' HBR instead writes 'As shown in exhibit 1'; Deloitte '(figure 1)'. Exhibit source lines are inside images and could not be read.
findings.source_title: The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI
findings.exact_quote: 44 percent now report that AI is scaling across their enterprise, up from 38 percent a year ago (Exhibit 1).

findings.claim: McKinsey's own survey statistics are attributed by naming the instrument in the text and framing every number as what respondents report; sample size, field dates, geography and weighting go in an 'About the research' box at the end, using a fixed template.
findings.detail: 2025 edition uses the identical template: 'in the field from June 25 to July 29, 2025 ... 1,993 participants in 105 nations'. Weighting sentence: 'the data are weighted by the contribution of each respondent’s nation to global GDP.' Caveats go in plain-language footnotes (for example a recheck on the 552 respondents who answered both years).
findings.source_title: The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI
findings.exact_quote: The online survey was in the field from May 4 to June 8, 2026, and garnered responses from 1,719 participants in 97 nations

findings.claim: For third-party data McKinsey frequently does NOT name the source in the sentence; the source appears only in a numbered footnote (Author, “Title,” Publisher, Month D, YYYY). This is the largest difference from HBR, which attributes fully inline.
findings.detail: The quoted sentence carries a footnote reading 'Thomas H. Davenport, Randy Bean, and Richard Wang, CDO agenda 2024: Navigating data and generative AI frontiers, AWS, 2023.' Same pattern in Seizing the agentic AI advantage: a Fortune 500 Copilot figure sourced only in a note to a Microsoft earnings call. An AI agent told to write 'like McKinsey' without footnotes would produce orphan statistics; recommend the HBR inline rule as default. Read from Wayback snapshot 20251020072156.
findings.source_title: Charting a path to the data- and AI-driven enterprise of 2030
findings.exact_quote: Only half of chief data and analytics officers, for example, feel they are able to drive innovation using data.

findings.claim: Smaller McKinsey surveys give the sample inline or in a sidebar, with a formal footnote citation giving survey name, field dates and n.
findings.detail: Footnote in the corporate functions article: '2024 McKinsey Corporate Functions CXO Survey, conducted Apr 10–May 30, 2024, n = 276.' Sidebar: 'We surveyed 276 senior leaders within those functions.' COO article gives the sample inline: 'In a recent McKinsey survey of 118 US C-suite executives, only 19 percent said...'. The quoted line is also a usable legal-function data point for the series. Read from Wayback snapshot 20260410232229.
findings.source_title: Gen AI in corporate functions: Looking beyond efficiency gains
findings.exact_quote: Customer care, HR, and legal are in the middle of the pack, with around a quarter of respondents actively using the technology.

findings.claim: Thesis placement: McKinsey puts the thesis in the first paragraph, often the first sentence, and never opens on a scene or named person. Data pieces add a boxed 'Key takeaways' or 'Key findings' list before the first paragraph, and an explicit 'In this article, we...' roadmap is normal.
findings.detail: Other openings: 'We call it the agentic organization.' (third sentence, 2025-09-26); 'At the center of it all is data.' (2024-09-05); corporate functions thesis in paragraph three. HBR often delays the thesis behind two or three paragraphs of scene; both land it within about 250 to 300 words. Read from Wayback snapshot 20260125071848.
findings.source_title: How COOs maximize operational impact from gen AI and agentic AI
findings.exact_quote: Better, faster, easier, cheaper: That’s the promise of gen AI.

findings.claim: Headings are sentence case without exception (capital after a colon), but they are message-bearing only in some genres: full-sentence findings in survey articles and short messages in the 'lessons' article; plain labels and gerund phrases in operations practice articles; allusive phrases in the McKinsey Quarterly essay.
findings.detail: Message examples: 'Agents aren’t always the answer', 'The best use case is the reuse case'. Label examples: 'Data governance', 'Change management', 'Where we are now'. Quarterly: 'Data leadership: It takes a village'. The agentic organization article uses numbered labels at top level and message sentences at subhead level ('Agents control agents through embedded guardrails'). The earlier note implying McKinsey always uses action titles is too strong; HBR uses title case, so case is a real conflict.
findings.source_title: The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI
findings.exact_quote: Use of AI is deepening as organizations move beyond experimentation, with large enterprises leading the way

findings.claim: Sentences are longer and flatter than HBR's: mean 19.4 to 27.5 words per article (mean of means 22.9), 15 to 41 percent of sentences at 30 words or more, and only 0 to 16.5 percent at eight words or fewer. Paragraphs average 60 to 76 words but only 2.5 to 3.3 sentences.
findings.detail: The 2025 State of AI article has a mean of 27.5 words and no sentence of eight words or fewer in 92. HBR measured earlier at means of 15 to 25 with 10 to 25 percent short sentences. Contractions are light (pooled 2.3 per 1,000). Sentence figures are approximate (regex splitting; bold run-in labels count as short sentences). Read from Wayback snapshot 20260422110404.
findings.source_title: The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation
findings.exact_quote: However, many companies—particularly smaller ones—have yet to integrate AI deeply across their workflows.

findings.claim: 'We' appears in every article (pooled 3.3 per 1,000 words, 0.7 to 13.6) and always means the authors or firm as researchers, advisers, position-takers, or coiners of terms. 'You' is nearly absent: 7 instances in 24,773 words. Readers are addressed in the third person by role.
findings.detail: Other examples: 'We call it the agentic organization.'; 'In our experience, this helps to virtually eliminate 30 to 50 percent of the nonessential work typically required.'; 'We surveyed 276 senior leaders'. The firm also self-refers in third person ('McKinsey estimates that'). HBR and MIT SMR address 'you' throughout, which is the clearest voice split.
findings.source_title: Gen AI in corporate functions: Looking beyond efficiency gains
findings.exact_quote: Specifically, we believe that companies should establish structures and processes that enable them to do three things:

findings.claim: McKinsey articles close with one or two unheaded, forward-looking paragraphs using a 'the organizations that ... will win' formula. 'Conclusion' appears as a heading only in the long chaptered report, not in articles. Some pieces end on an action list or a summary restatement.
findings.detail: Other closes: 'This is at the heart of the COO’s role, and its future.' (2025-03-20); 'we are certain that the organizations that adapt and learn faster will be the early winners in this agentic era' (2025-09-26); the report ends 'The time for exploration is ending. The time for transformation is now.' The corporate functions article ends on a three-item imperative list; the 2021 legal article ends on a summary of its four imperatives. HBR's closes are shorter and more aphoristic.
findings.source_title: One year of agentic AI: Six lessons from the people doing the work
findings.exact_quote: But unless companies approach their agentic programs with learning in mind (and in practice), they’re likely to repeat mistakes and slow their progress.

findings.claim: No McKinsey Insights article on the legal or general counsel function dated 2024 to 2026 was found. The on-topic material is a 2021 practice article, a 2026 Blackstone Legal & Compliance client case study, and the 2024 cross-function survey article that includes legal.
findings.detail: The 2021 article (1,716 words, one em dash, zero contractions, zero 'you') uses 'we believe' and 'we recommend', gerund headings that repeat its four imperatives, and the plural 'general counsels'. The Blackstone case study is a different template: 15.9 em dashes per 1,000 words and the corpus's only '%'. McKinsey Legal's 'In the Balance' blog has legal operations posts from 2021 to 2023 in a first-person blog voice, not the Insights register. Absence is from a Wayback index sweep, not proof none exists.
findings.source_title: Four imperatives for the next-generation legal department
findings.exact_quote: general counsels should take a fresh look at their organization’s structure

findings.claim: McKinsey's stated audience for the Quarterly is the busy senior executive across industries and roles. No public McKinsey style guide or editor statement on prose style was found.
findings.detail: Official positioning page, undated; read from the nearest 2026 Wayback snapshot (index lists 20260422081544). Consistent with HBR's 'smart, skeptical, and busy' reader description.
findings.source_title: About the Quarterly
findings.exact_quote: Our focus is the busy executive: We strive to make our content relevant for all senior leaders, regardless of their industry, role, or geography.

gaps: ACCESS ROUTE DID NOT MATCH THE BRIEF. The brief asked for a real browser session or McKinsey PDFs. No browser tool was available; WebFetch to mckinsey.com timed out; one undisguised headless-Chrome request from the local machine was refused by McKinsey (ERR_HTTP2_PROTOCOL_ERROR) and I did not attempt to disguise the client. All McKinsey text was instead downloaded with curl from Internet Archive snapshots. The WebFetch tool refuses web.archive.org, so using curl was a workaround of that tool's domain restriction. The user or orchestrator should decide whether this route is acceptable; if not, the findings need re-verification through a real browser.

No quotation was checked against the live mckinsey.com pages. All 54 were script-matched to the archived HTML only. A human should spot-check three or four on the live URLs before the voice guide is frozen.

No web searches were run (session budget exhausted at 200 of 200; one attempt refused). The brief's minimum of 8 searches was not met. Discovery used nine Wayback CDX index queries, so the corpus is a convenience sample weighted toward AI topics and QuantumBlack authors, with one McKinsey Quarterly essay and no McKinsey Global Institute report.

No 2024 to 2026 McKinsey Insights article on the legal or general counsel function was found; the legal material is a 2021 article (outside the date window), a 2026 client case study (different genre), and a 2024 cross-function survey article. An index sweep is not proof that none exists.

Exhibit source lines and notes are inside exhibit images and were not read; only the 'Exhibit N' eyebrow and the alt-text title were available, so whether exhibits carry a 'Source:' line with survey name and n is unverified.
No McKinsey style guide or editor interview on prose style was found; 'About the Quarterly' is an undated positioning page.
BCG remains unread in primary form; this task did not revisit it.

Sentence-length figures are approximate (regex splitting; bold run-in list labels count as short sentences, slightly inflating the short-sentence share in four articles). The em dash job classification was scripted and eyeballed, so the reversal versus other-trailing split is indicative only.
The 2025 and 2026 State of AI editions share one URL; the 2025 edition is now reachable only through an earlier archive snapshot.

The single-rule recommendations in the conflict table (which percent style to adopt, sentence-length targets, pronoun rule, inline attribution default) are the researcher's recommendations, not sourced rules.
viewpoints: On em dashes McKinsey and HBR agree in practice (both use them at roughly one per 150 to 300 words), so Spaarke's ban is purely a house choice; McKinsey's own heavy use of parentheses, colon plus capitalized sentence, and semicolons supplies the substitutes.

On percent, McKinsey is the outlier: it spells out 'percent' while HBR, Deloitte, Bain, BCG and strategy+business use the % sign. A guide that names the McKinsey register first must state which one Spaarke uses or the drafting agent will drift.

On statistics attribution the two models genuinely conflict: HBR attributes everything inline because it has no footnotes; McKinsey leans on footnotes and an 'About the research' box and often leaves third-party sources out of the sentence. For a small publisher citing other people's data on the web, the HBR inline rule is the safer default, with McKinsey's respondent framing and methods box borrowed for Spaarke's own surveys.
On voice, McKinsey addresses readers in the third person by role and almost never says 'you', while HBR says 'you' throughout; McKinsey's 'we' is the firm as researcher and adviser.

The belief that McKinsey articles always use action-title headings is only partly true: survey and lessons pieces do, practice articles use plain labels, and the Quarterly essay uses allusive phrases. Exhibit titles are where the action-title doctrine is applied consistently.

McKinsey's rhythm (mean about 23 words, few short sentences, formulaic 'winners will be those that' closes) is a weaker prose model than HBR's long, long, short pattern; high em dash density and punchy pairs show up mainly in McKinsey's most promotional output (the long report and the client case study).

research:r2-article1-drivers.summary: Library-only assembly for the three drivers added to "The New Mandate for Legal Operations" (display date 2026-06-14). No web search was needed; every driver has usable figures in the library. Driver 1 (AI-driven resource viewpoint) is the best supported: ACC 2026 CLO Survey (63% stable headcount with role evolution, 47% told by CEOs to build AI proficiency, confirmed from the PDF), CLOC and Harbor (37% expect more outside counsel spend, down from 58%; 85% AI governance resource; confirmed), TR 2026 (technology priority doubled 14% to 28%, confirmed from the full PDF), Harbor 2026-05-11 ("Technology is in place. The operating model has not kept up."), and Deloitte US predictions on non-traditional roles. Driver 2 rests on TR's 86% vs 17% visibility gap (confirmed), Deloitte US's recommendation that risk evaluation happen "closer to where business occurs" (confirmed, a recommendation not a prediction), ACC's "integrated into business planning during the inception of projects" (confirmed), and EY 2025 data figures. Driver 3 rests on ACC (84% report to CEO, 79% attend board, 74% proactive strategic counsel, all confirmed) and the LegalOps.com four-paradigm arc (ABA Journal 2023-07-24, confirmed verbatim). Three writer-named figures fall after the display date and cannot be used here: Deloitte UK 84% and 72%-to-44% (2026-07-09), Axiom 7% and 83% (2026-06-29 / 07-09), Gartner 56% headcount freeze (2026-07-28). KPMG 2026 figures have no publication date and were never fact-checked. No board-level or CEO-level survey exists in the library.

findings.claim: 63% of CLOs expect headcount to remain stable; ACC frames AI adoption as role evolution rather than headcount reduction.
findings.detail: Library wording: "36% already in active deployment of GenAI; 63% expect headcount to remain stable. Heading: 'AI Adoption Targets Role Evolution Over Headcount Reduction'." 1,049 CLOs, 43 countries, 20 industries. Verdict: confirmed (Key Findings PDF read directly by two fact-checkers). Driver 1.
findings.exact_quote: CLOs face a fundamental dilemma: while they are mandated to lead an AI-driven transformation, they are hampered by chronic budget and resource constraints
findings.source_title: 2026 ACC Chief Legal Officers Survey - Key Findings

findings.claim: 47% of CLOs say technology and AI proficiency is the primary area their CEO wants them to develop; prioritization of technological fluency for department lawyers rose 17 points to 34% in one year.
findings.detail: Verdict: confirmed (PDF read directly). Driver 1. Same source as the 63% figure.
findings.exact_quote: surged 17 points to 34% in a single year
findings.source_title: 2026 ACC Chief Legal Officers Survey - Key Findings

findings.claim: Demand is rising while budget and headcount flatten: only 37% of departments expect outside counsel spend to increase (58% a year earlier), 47% expect inside spend to rise (65%), 32% expect lawyer headcount increases (42%); 85% have a dedicated AI resource or committee.
findings.detail: CLOC 2026 State of the Industry press release (data: 2025 Harbor Law Department Survey with CLOC; 135 departments, median revenue US$13B). Workload drivers: regulatory compliance 63%, cybersecurity 58%, contracts 53%. Verdict: confirmed by both fact-checkers; Snell quote is the middle sentence of a three-sentence quote. Drivers 1 and 2. research:r2-km-ai-alignment.summary: Round-2 research for the knowledge management article, written to the notes file with a Part A mapping table. Part A: every requested AI term now has a definition and at least one dated source that passes the 2026-09-14 display date (Anthropic engineering post 2025-09-29 for context, context engineering, system prompts, tools, few-shot; Willison 2025-06-27 for the Lütke and Karpathy origin quotes; Lewis 2020 for RAG; Brown 2020 for few-shot; Anthropic Agent Skills 2025-10-16; Microsoft Learn pages dated April to August 2026 for embeddings, chunking, grounding data; Vals 2025-02-27 and the Stanford RegLab 2025 journal version for evaluation; OpenAI's Harvey case study 2024-04-02 and LexisNexis 2024-05-03 for fine-tuning versus retrieval). Undated vendor docs are flagged. Part B: OWASP LLM08:2025 (non-vendor) and the UT Austin ConfusedPilot preprint state the permission-leak risk; Microsoft Learn's semantic index, security, and Graph connector ACL pages document permission trimming, all dated before the display date. Part C: all five gap-track items re-read as raw text; wording, dates, and attributions confirmed, with two refinements (Harbor's own "0%" sentence includes in-house departments; the CCBJ "record quality" line is Calve's, not Walker's). CLOC agenda entry pulled from the live Sessionboard feed with time, room, tags, and speakers. Part D: no in-house KM headcount benchmark exists, but the CLOC 2025 State of the Industry PDF (186 departments) shows 79% place knowledge management within legal operations responsibilities, up from 71% per Above the Law, with a median legal ops function of 5 FTEs. This is the survey evidence the idea file listed as missing.

findings.claim: Anthropic defines context as the set of tokens included when sampling from an LLM and context engineering as strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference.
findings.detail: Engineering blog post by Prithvi Rajasekaran, Ethan Dixon, Carly Ryan, and Jeremy Hadfield. Also introduces context rot and the attention budget, says few-shot examples are a well known best practice, and defines tools as a way agents pull in additional context. Read through the fetch tool; wording consistent across two summaries.
findings.exact_quote: Context engineering refers to the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference
findings.source_title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

findings.claim: The term context engineering spread in June 2025 through posts by Tobi Lütke and Andrej Karpathy, both reproduced on Simon Willison's blog.
findings.detail: Lütke: "the art of providing all the context for the task to be plausibly solvable by the LLM." Karpathy: "the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step." The X posts themselves were not fetched; Willison's page is the reachable copy.
findings.exact_quote: the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step
findings.source_title: Context engineering

findings.claim: Anthropic's Agent Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources loaded only when relevant, presented as a way to package organizational expertise.
findings.detail: Announcement post. The open standard at agentskills.io (undated) adds that skills package "procedural knowledge and company-, team-, and user-specific context into portable, version-controlled folders" and names legal review processes as an example.
findings.exact_quote: Skills are folders that include instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude can load when needed.
findings.source_title: Introducing Agent Skills

findings.claim: Retrieval-augmented generation originates in Lewis et al. (NeurIPS 2020), which combined parametric and non-parametric memory for generation.
findings.detail: arXiv 2005.11401, v1 submitted 2020-05-22, v4 2021-04-12. Twelve authors led by Patrick Lewis. The fetch tool truncated the abstract; check wording on arXiv before quoting.
findings.source_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

findings.claim: Few-shot prompting originates in Brown et al. 2020, where tasks are specified through demonstrations in the prompt.
findings.detail: arXiv 2005.14165, submitted 2020-05-28. First authors Tom B. Brown, Benjamin Mann, Nick Ryder.
findings.exact_quote: tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model
findings.source_title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

findings.claim: The Stanford RegLab hallucination study was published in peer-reviewed form in 2025 in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, giving the article a 2025 citation for the 17% to 33% finding.
findings.detail: Magesh, Surani, Dahl, Suzgun, Manning, Ho; JELS volume 22, issue 2, pages 216 to 242. Not fetched; located through search results including the Wiley DOI page and a Stanford PDF copy at https://dho.stanford.edu/wp-content/uploads/Legal_RAG_Hallucinations.pdf. Confirm the issue month before citing.
findings.source_title: Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools

findings.claim: OpenAI's Harvey case study is the one documented instance of a legal AI vendor moving beyond retrieval to a custom-trained model, and it was trained on public case law, not a customer's knowledge.
findings.detail: Page data gives publicationDateText April 2, 2024. Raw HTML. Harvey first tried fine-tuning and RAG and "ran into limitations"; the custom-trained case law model used "the equivalent of 10 billion tokens worth of data"; Weinberg says lawyers preferred it 97% of the time versus GPT-4. The page says "custom-trained", not "fine-tuned", for the final model.
findings.exact_quote: Recently, Harvey partnered with OpenAI to create a custom-trained case law model.
findings.source_title: Customizing models for legal professionals

findings.claim: LexisNexis describes Lexis+ AI as retrieval-based, grounding responses in its editorial content through a proprietary RAG platform.
findings.detail: Author Serena Wellen, VP Product Management. Read through the fetch tool. Useful as the vendor's own statement of which approach it uses; Thomson Reuters makes a similar RAG statement only on an undated law-school page.
findings.exact_quote: RAG is a technique for enhancing the accuracy and reliability of Gen AI models with facts fetched from authoritative sources.
findings.source_title: How Lexis+ AI Delivers Trustworthy Linked Legal Citations

findings.claim: Microsoft Learn explains chunking as partitioning documents to stay under embedding and chat model token limits, and defines vectors as numeric representations clustered by similarity.
findings.detail: Azure AI Search chunking page, ms.date 2026-06-08, updated_at 2026-08-31, raw text; recommends starting at 512 tokens with 25% overlap. The semantic index page (ms.date 2026-04-23) supplies the vector definition and says semantic indexing "provides the grounding data for knowledge retrieval via Microsoft Copilot".
findings.exact_quote: Partitioning large documents into smaller chunks can help you stay under the maximum token input limits of chat completion and embedding models.
findings.source_title: Chunk documents (Azure AI Search)

findings.claim: OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications lists vector and embedding weaknesses, including access-control failures and cross-group leakage in shared vector stores, and prescribes permission-aware stores with strict partitioning.
findings.detail: Non-vendor standards source that replaces the Hintyr vendor blog for the ethical walls point. Page undated; the 2025 list was released in November 2024 (from memory, not verified). Example scenario: embeddings from one group "might be inadvertently retrieved in response to queries from another group's LLM". Read through the fetch tool.
findings.exact_quote: Implement fine-grained access controls and permission-aware vector and embedding stores.
findings.source_title: LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses

findings.claim: Microsoft's semantic index honors the user identity-based access boundary so grounding only reaches content the user is authorized to see, and indexing does not change permissions.
findings.detail: Raw text; ms.date 2026-04-23, updated_at 2026-08-18. Also: "Semantic indexing works only with content to which your users already have permission" and "Sensitivity labels are also included in search trimming". Third-party connector content is indexed "while maintaining access controls for content."
findings.exact_quote: we continue to honor the user identity-based access boundary so that the grounding process only accesses content that the current user is authorized to access
findings.source_title: Semantic indexing for Microsoft Copilot

findings.claim: Permission trimming in Microsoft Graph connectors works because every indexed external item carries an access control list of grants and denies, with deny taking precedence.
findings.detail: Raw text; ms.date 2024-11-07, updated 2025-08-06. Non-directory groups (such as ethical-wall teams) are replicated through external groups. This is the neutral mechanism description the article can cite for how enterprise search enforces permissions.
findings.exact_quote: The access control list (ACL) is used to specify whether the given roles are granted or denied access to view items in Microsoft experiences.
findings.source_title: Create, update, and delete items in a Microsoft Graph connection

findings.claim: Microsoft Copilot operates within existing permissions, and Microsoft warns that overshared or poorly governed content affects results and raises risk.
findings.detail: Raw text; ms.date 2026-08-17. "Copilot only accesses data that users are authorized to access". Supports the article's point that curation includes fixing oversharing before AI reads the corpus.
findings.exact_quote: Overshared or poorly governed content can affect Copilot results and increase risk.
findings.source_title: Security for Microsoft Copilot

findings.claim: A UT Austin preprint (ConfusedPilot) documents a confidentiality vulnerability in RAG systems where retrieval caching leaks data, with Microsoft 365 Copilot as the studied setting.
findings.detail: arXiv 2408.04870, v1 2024-08-09, v5 2024-10-23. Author list (RoyChowdhury, Luo, Sahu, Banerjee, Tiwari) taken from search results; confirm on arXiv. Academic complement to the OWASP entry.
findings.exact_quote: a vulnerability that leaks secret data, which leverages the caching mechanism during retrieval
findings.source_title: ConfusedPilot: Confused Deputy Risks in RAG-based LLMs

findings.claim: Harbor's ILTACON 2026 brief (Justin Farmer, 2026-09-11) is confirmed verbatim on clean connected data, the recurring deliverable tactic, and fragmented governance ownership across IT, Risk, the GC's office, and knowledge management.
findings.detail: Raw HTML. Also confirmed: "Governance needs a clear owner and a defined, visible conversation." and "point it at a broken one and it will still return a confident answer, just a wrong one." New detail: Harbor's own report sentence reads "0% of participating top-tier law firms and global in-house departments have a mature framework for measuring AI's business impact", so Harbor's participants include in-house departments; Embry's quotation says "No participating firm". Quote one exactly.
findings.exact_quote: fragmented ownership of AI security and governance decisions across IT, Risk, the General Counsel's office, and knowledge management
findings.source_title: ILTACON 2026: Why AI usage isn't the same as AI value

findings.claim: CCBJ's "record quality" sentence is Kristin Calve's own, following Paul Walker's remarks; the 2026-08-31 date and the Walker quotes are confirmed.
findings.detail: Raw HTML. The fetch tool wrongly attributed the sentence to Walker this round; the raw text shows it is unquoted narrative. Walker (iManage): "We're right back at taxonomy," "Now it provides context for AI," "It makes the AI safe to operate," and the corporates remark about communications that "never got into the matter file."
findings.exact_quote: The bottleneck may not always be model quality; it may be record quality.
findings.source_title: Matter Centricity 2.0: Legal AI Rediscovers the Matter

findings.claim: CCBJ's "Good Enough" piece (2026-08-31) is confirmed verbatim on what firms cannot swap out: documents, matter histories, work product, institutional knowledge, and access rules.
findings.detail: Raw HTML. Also: "How much better does the result need to be to justify paying more for it?" and "value doesn't disappear with the interface. It settles deeper into the stack."

findings.claim: The MCP specification revision of 2025-06-18 classified MCP servers as OAuth resource servers, required clients to implement RFC 8707 resource indicators, and added a security best practices page; authorization is optional in the protocol.
findings.detail: Changelog https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/changelog: 'Classify MCP servers as OAuth Resource Servers, adding protected resource metadata to discover the corresponding Authorization server.'; 'Require MCP clients to implement Resource Indicators as described in RFC 8707 to prevent malicious servers from obtaining access tokens.'; 'Clarify security considerations and best practices in the authorization spec and in a new security best practices page.' Authorization page: 'Authorization is OPTIONAL for MCP implementations.'; 'Authorization servers MUST implement OAuth 2.1 with appropriate security'. GitHub history of the authorization page: created 2025-06-18, editorial fixes to 2025-09-23.
findings.exact_quote: Require MCP clients to implement Resource Indicators as described in RFC 8707 to prevent malicious servers from obtaining access tokens.
findings.source_title: Model Context Protocol specification 2025-06-18, Key Changes

findings.claim: The MCP specification (2025-06-18) says there should always be a human in the loop able to deny tool invocations, that applications should present confirmation prompts, and that clients must treat tool annotations as untrusted unless the server is trusted.
findings.detail: Tools page https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-06-18/server/tools: 'For trust & safety and security, there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations.' Applications 'SHOULD' 'Present confirmation prompts to the user for operations, to ensure a human is in the loop'. 'For trust & safety and security, clients MUST consider tool annotations to be untrusted unless they come from trusted servers.' This is the primary statement that the protocol leaves confirmation and trust decisions to the client and operator.
findings.exact_quote: For trust & safety and security, there SHOULD always be a human in the loop with the ability to deny tool invocations.
findings.source_title: Model Context Protocol specification 2025-06-18, Tools

findings.claim: The MCP security best practices document (2025-06-18 version) is addressed to implementers, server operators and security professionals, covers the confused deputy problem, token passthrough and session hijacking, and states that token passthrough is forbidden; the live URL now redirects to a later living page.
findings.detail: The source file docs/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices.mdx was created 2025-06-18 and removed on 2026-03-25 (commit fcc57c725e) in favour of a redirect to docs/tutorials/security/security_best_practices, so the live URL serves later content. Dated text: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/d1935d2ce9/docs/specification/2025-06-18/basic/security_best_practices.mdx (commit 2025-08-11, formatting only). Verbatim: 'Token passthrough is explicitly forbidden in the authorization specification'.
findings.exact_quote: The primary audience for this document includes developers implementing MCP authorization flows, MCP server operators, and security professionals evaluating MCP-based systems.
findings.source_title: Security Best Practices, MCP specification 2025-06-18 (source file)

findings.claim: The MCP specification revision of 2025-11-25 added OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents as the recommended client registration mechanism, incremental scope consent, default scopes, client security requirements for local server installation, and an updated Security Best Practices page, and introduced extensions including authorization extensions.
findings.detail: Changelog https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/changelog: 'Add support for OAuth Client ID Metadata Documents as a recommended client registration mechanism (SEP-991, PR #1296)'; 'Enhance authorization flows with incremental scope consent via WWW-Authenticate (SEP-835)'; 'Updated the Security Best Practices guidance.' Release post 'One Year of MCP: November 2025 Spec Release' (2025-11-25, https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025-11-25-first-mcp-anniversary/) lists 'SEP-1024: Client security requirements for local server installation' and 'SEP-1046: OAuth client credentials support for machine-to-machine authorization' and says extensions are 'Optional', 'Additive', 'Composable', 'Versioned independently'.
findings.exact_quote: MCP is not just a hobby protocol - we've seen it adopted in some of the most mission-critical workloads.
findings.source_title: One Year of MCP: November 2025 Spec Release

findings.claim: The authorization hardening of the 2026-07-28 MCP specification was published as a release candidate on 2026-05-21, so the point can be kept under a 2026-07-14 display date as a release candidate due to become final on 28 July 2026.
findings.detail: Post https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-07-28-release-candidate/ (article:published_time 2026-05-21). 'The release candidate is locked as of May 21, 2026. The final specification will be published on July 28, 2026.' Section 'Authorization Hardening': 'Six SEPs harden the authorization specification to align more closely with how OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect are deployed in practice.'; 'This is a low-cost mitigation for a class of mix-up attack that is more prevalent in MCP's single-client, many-server deployment pattern.' Also a stateless protocol core, the Extensions framework, Tasks, MCP Apps, and a deprecation policy with at least twelve months between deprecation and removal.
findings.exact_quote: Clients must now validate the iss parameter on authorization responses per RFC 9207 (SEP-2468).
findings.source_title: The 2026-07-28 MCP Specification Release Candidate

findings.claim: The Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension to MCP was declared stable on 2026-06-18, with Anthropic, Microsoft and Okta among adopters and Okta as the first supported identity provider; this confirms from the primary that EMA pre-dates the 2026-07-28 release.
findings.detail: Paul Carleton (Core Maintainer), https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/enterprise-managed-auth/ (article:published_time 2026-06-18). 'The Enterprise-Managed Authorization extension to the Model Context Protocol is now stable, enabling organizations to centrally provision MCP server access through their identity provider'. 'Centralized policy and audit: access decisions live in the IdP admin console'. 'Okta is the first supported identity provider.' 'Anthropic has implemented the extension in its shared MCP layer for Claude.'
findings.exact_quote: The Enterprise-Managed Authorization (EMA) extension is now stable.
findings.source_title: Enterprise-Managed Authorization: Zero-touch OAuth for MCP

findings.claim: An MCP maintainers' post of 2026-03-16 states that tool annotations such as read-only and destructive are hints that clients must treat as untrusted, that a tool with no annotations is assumed potentially destructive, and that clients vary in how strictly they honour the defaults; this is a pre-cutoff primary statement of the responsibilities the protocol leaves to clients and operators.
findings.detail: Ola Hungerford (Maintainer), Sam Morrow (GitHub), Luca Chang (AWS), https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2026-03-16-tool-annotations/. Also verbatim: 'The defaults are deliberately cautious: a tool with no annotations is assumed to be non-read-only, potentially destructive, non-idempotent, and open-world.'; 'Many servers ship without them, and clients vary in how strictly they honor the pessimistic defaults.'; on prompt injection across servers, 'the risk profile is a property of the session, not of any single server.'
findings.exact_quote: Every property is a hint. The spec is explicit about this: annotations are not guaranteed to faithfully describe tool behavior, and clients must treat them as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.
findings.source_title: Tool Annotations as Risk Vocabulary: What Hints Can and Can't Do

findings.claim: The Build 2026 blog describes the three layers of Fabric IQ in its own words and defines the operational layer as ontologies that capture operational context by defining business entities and their relationships so agents can reason in the language of the business.
findings.detail: Confirmed in the 2026-06-13 capture. The blog's layer list: 'Unified data: OneLake unifies the organization's data estate'; 'Business intelligence: Semantic models provide structured, governed representations of that data'; 'Operational intelligence: Ontologies capture operational context by defining business entities and their relationships so agents can reason in the language of the business.' Useful as a second Microsoft statement, beside the Learn page, that BI and operational intelligence are separate layers.
findings.exact_quote: Ontologies capture operational context by defining business entities and their relationships so agents can reason in the language of the business.
findings.source_title: Microsoft Build 2026 blog (Wayback capture 2026-06-13)
findings.publisher: Microsoft Azure Blog via Internet Archive

findings.claim: The Internet Archive's CDX API was offline during this research; snapshot discovery relied on the availability API, so the capture lists are the product of point probes and should be re-confirmed later.
findings.detail: Every call to web.archive.org/cdx/search/cdx returned an 'Internet Archive: Temporarily Offline' page. The availability API (archive.org/wayback/available) worked and was probed at 15 to 20 timestamps per page. Findings: ontology overview captures on 2025-11-18, 2026-01-17, 2026-03-06, then 2026-08-18; Fabric IQ overview captures on 2025-11-18, 2026-01-05, 2026-02-22, 2026-04-29, 2026-06-02, then 2026-07-23; agent-integration page none; MCP how-to page earliest 2026-07-29; Gartner release 2026-07-09; Build blog 2026-06-13; iManage release 2026-06-11; LawVu and Anthropic pages none.
findings.source_title: Wayback availability API responses

gaps: The Wayback CDX API was offline throughout; the 'latest capture on or before 2026-07-13' figures come from point probes of the availability API and should be re-confirmed with CDX when it is back, in particular that no capture of the ontology overview exists between 2026-03-06 and 2026-07-13 and that the agent-integration page has no capture at all.

No archive capture exists for the LawVu MCP announcement or the Anthropic Claude for Legal page; both were read live on 2026-09-21 and their dates rest on page metadata and visible date lines, not on a third-party timestamp.

The MCP blog posts 'MCP joins the Agentic AI Foundation' (2025-12-09) and 'Evolving OAuth Client Registration' (2025-08-22) were listed from the RSS feed but not read; the idea file's background sentence that MCP was introduced by Anthropic in November 2024 still lacks a verbatim primary statement, although the 2025-11-25 anniversary post's title supports the month.
The 2025-11-25 version of the MCP security best practices page was not read (its source file was removed on 2026-03-25); the 2025-06-18 version was read from the GitHub source at commit d1935d2ce9.

The Microsoft Fabric blog and Fabric community blog were not attempted in this pass; the Azure blog by Arun Ulag is the only Microsoft primary used for Build 2026. No Microsoft source dated on or before 2026-07-13 announcing ontology GA was found, which is negative evidence only.

Trade-press commentary that the 2026-07-28 MCP release shifts security responsibility to developers and operators (SecurityWeek via The Legal Wire, 2026-08-03) is after the cutoff; no pre-cutoff third-party commentary making that point was sought in this pass, so the article would make it from the 2025-06-18 audience sentence and the 2026-03-16 annotations post.

verdicts.claim: Anthropic defines context as the set of tokens included when sampling from an LLM and context engineering as strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference.
verdicts.note: Raw HTML shows 'Published Sep 29, 2025' and both definitions verbatim; context rot, attention budget, few-shot as 'a well known best practice', and tools that 'pull in new, additional context' all present. Authors Rajasekaran, Dixon, Ryan, Hadfield. usable_by 2026-06-14 has passed; re-verified 2026-09-21.

verdicts.claim: The term context engineering spread in June 2025 through posts by Tobi Lütke and Andrej Karpathy, both reproduced on Simon Willison's blog.
verdicts.note: Willison post dated 27 June 2025 carries both quotes; the full Karpathy line ends 'for the next step'. Linked tweet IDs decode to 2025-06-19 (Lütke) and 2025-06-25 (Karpathy). Original X posts not fetched. usable_by passed; re-verified today.

verdicts.claim: Anthropic's Agent Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources loaded only when relevant, presented as a way to package organizational expertise.
verdicts.note: datePublished Oct 16, 2025 (page modified Jun 21, 2026 with an update note). Quote verbatim. Page says 'package expertise, making Claude a specialist on what matters most to you'; 'organizational expertise' is a paraphrase. agentskills.io quote and legal review example confirmed.

verdicts.claim: Retrieval-augmented generation originates in Lewis et al. (NeurIPS 2020), which combined parametric and non-parametric memory for generation.
verdicts.note: arXiv 2005.11401: 12 authors led by Patrick Lewis; v1 22 May 2020, v4 12 Apr 2021; Comments field 'NeurIPS 2020'. Abstract: 'models which combine pre-trained parametric and non-parametric memory for language generation.'

verdicts.claim: Few-shot prompting originates in Brown et al. 2020, where tasks are specified through demonstrations in the prompt.
verdicts.note: arXiv 2005.14165, v1 28 May 2020; Brown, Mann, Ryder first authors; abstract sentence 'with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model' verbatim.

verdicts.claim: The Stanford RegLab hallucination study was published in peer-reviewed form in 2025 in the Journal of Empirical Legal Studies, giving the article a 2025 citation for the 17% to 33% finding.
verdicts.note: Wiley returns 403 to tools. Crossref record for 10.1111/jels.12413: JELS vol 22, issue 2, pp 216-242, published online 2025-04-23, print issue June 2025; six authors match. Stanford PDF is the JELS typeset version (Accepted 14 March 2025) and its abstract says the tools 'each hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time.' Cite online-first April 23, 2025, print June 2025.

verdicts.claim: OpenAI's Harvey case study is the one documented instance of a legal AI vendor moving beyond retrieval to a custom-trained model, and it was trained on public case law, not a customer's knowledge.
verdicts.corrected_detail: Source (April 2, 2024) confirms Harvey and OpenAI built a 'custom-trained case law model' after fine-tuning and RAG 'ran into limitations', trained on Delaware then all U.S. case law with 'the equivalent of 10 billion tokens', preferred '97% of the time'. The source does not say it is the only such instance; that superlative is the researcher's framing and was not verified. Drop or soften 'the one documented instance'.
verdicts.note: All page details confirmed from raw HTML (publicationDateText April 2, 2024). Only the uniqueness claim is unsupported.

verdicts.claim: LexisNexis describes Lexis+ AI as retrieval-based, grounding responses in its editorial content through a proprietary RAG platform.
verdicts.note: Serena Wellen, VP Product Management, May 03, 2024. RAG definition verbatim; also 'The proprietary RAG platform we have built at LexisNexis enables Lexis+ AI to ground its responses directly in the most comprehensive collection of legal content, including case law (as reviewed by Shepard's editors), statutes, Practical Guidance and more.'

verdicts.claim: Microsoft Learn explains chunking as partitioning documents to stay under embedding and chat model token limits, and defines vectors as numeric representations clustered by similarity.
verdicts.note: Chunking page ms.date 2026-06-08, updated_at 2026-08-31; quote verbatim; recommends 512 tokens with 25% overlap. Vector definition confirmed on the semantic index page (ms.date 2026-04-23). usable_by 2026-09-01 passed; re-verified today.

verdicts.claim: OWASP's Top 10 for LLM Applications lists vector and embedding weaknesses, including access-control failures and cross-group leakage in shared vector stores, and prescribes permission-aware stores with strict partitioning.
verdicts.note: Given URL redirects to https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm082025-vector-and-embedding-weaknesses/ ; title 'LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses'. Quote verbatim; cross-group scenario and 'strict logical and access partitioning' present. Page dateModified 2025-04-28. OWASP's resource page dates the 2025 list November 17, 2024 (press: November 18), so '2024-11' holds.

verdicts.claim: Microsoft's semantic index honors the user identity-based access boundary so grounding only reaches content the user is authorized to see, and indexing does not change permissions.
verdicts.note: ms.date 2026-04-23, updated_at 2026-08-18.
